turns.ans: Your definition comes from your Defense mechanisms sticky note in My Notes. It lists projection alongside repression, displacement, rationalization and sublimation. The idea itself goes back to Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic theory, which Anna Freud later expanded on.

turns.expect: The id's drive to seek immediate gratification of instinctual drives, from their Freud note.
turns.ans:
The pleasure principle is Freud's idea that the id seeks immediate gratification of its drives and tries to avoid pain or tension. It wants what feels good now, with no regard for consequences.

The ego later works by the reality principle, which delays gratification until it's safe or appropriate. For example, a hungry infant cries until fed (pleasure principle), while an adult waits for a meal they can actually get.

turns.expect: The ego's principle: delaying/adapting gratification to what reality allows, mediating between the id and reality.
turns.ans: The reality principle is Freud's idea that the ego takes over from the pleasure principle and considers what's actually possible and safe in the outside world. It delays gratification, or changes how the drive is met, so that the person can get what they need without harm. For example, an adult who is hungry but has no food nearby waits until a meal is available, instead of demanding it right now like an infant would.

turns.q: is the id there from birth
turns.expect: Yes, their Freud note says the id is present from birth.
turns.ans: Yes. In Freud's model, the id is the only part of the personality present from birth. It is the primitive, unconscious part that seeks immediate gratification of instinctual drives, which is the pleasure principle. The ego develops later as the child deals with reality, and the superego forms as they internalize rules from parents and society. Your notes say the same: the id is present from birth.

turns.expect: From general knowledge: the ego develops in infancy as the child meets reality, the superego around age 3-5 (resolution of the Oedipal stage); says this is not in their note.
turns.ans: In Freud's model, the ego develops next, usually in early childhood, as the child begins to deal with reality. It is the rational part that mediates between the id and reality, which is the reality principle, and it uses defense mechanisms to do that. The superego develops after that, as the child internalizes rules from parents and society. It is the moral conscience and it causes guilt. Your notes list the same three parts, with the id present from birth and the ego and superego forming over time.

turns.expect: Systole (ventricles contract, eject blood) and diastole (ventricles relax and fill), resting HR 60-100, driven by SA node impulse through AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers, citing their note.
turns.ans:
The cardiac cycle is one complete heartbeat: the heart fills with blood, then pumps it out. It has two main phases.

Diastole is the relaxation and filling phase. The atria and ventricles relax, and blood flows in from the veins. The AV valves (between the atria and ventricles) are open. Most ventricular filling happens passively this way, before the atria contract.
Systole is the contraction phase. The atria contract first and top up the ventricles. Then the ventricles contract. Pressure rises until the AV valves close (the "lub" heart sound), and then the semilunar valves open to eject blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

In order, one cycle goes like this:

Atrial and ventricular diastole: the heart is relaxed, and blood flows passively into the atria and then the ventricles.
Atrial systole: the SA node fires, and the atria contract to push the remaining blood into the ventricles.
Ventricular systole: the ventricles contract. The AV valves close, then the semilunar valves open, and blood is ejected.
Ventricular diastole: the ventricles relax. The semilunar valves close (the "dub" sound), and the AV valves open again to start the next filling.

The electrical signal drives this sequence. It starts at the SA node, the natural pacemaker, and passes to the AV node, which briefly delays it so the atria finish before the ventricles contract. It then travels through the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibers, which make the ventricles contract from the bottom up.

turns.expect: Plain-language version: the heart squeezes (systole) to push blood out, then relaxes (diastole) to refill, with the SA node as the starter spark.
turns.ans:
Sure! Your heart works in a loop: it fills with blood, then squeezes it out, and repeats.

Filling (diastole): the heart relaxes and blood flows in.
Squeezing (systole): the heart contracts and pushes blood out to the lungs and the body.

An electrical signal runs the whole thing. It starts at the SA node, the heart's natural pacemaker, and travels through the heart so the top chambers squeeze first, then the bottom chambers.

A simple way to remember it: fill, then squeeze, then repeat.

turns.expect: SA node fires as pacemaker, impulse passes to AV node (delay), bundle of His, then Purkinje fibers which make the ventricles contract, from their Cardiac cycle note.
turns.ans:
The heart's conduction system is the electrical pathway that makes the chambers beat in a coordinated order:

SA node (sinoatrial node): in the right atrium, it sets the pace at about 60 to 100 beats per minute and starts each heartbeat. The impulse spreads across both atria, making them contract.
AV node (atrioventricular node): between the atria and ventricles, it briefly slows the signal, about 0.1 seconds, so the ventricles have time to fill with blood.
Bundle of His: the signal travels down the septum between the ventricles and splits into the left and right bundle branches.
Purkinje fibers: these spread through the ventricle walls, so the ventricles contract from the apex upward and push blood out to the lungs and body.

If the SA node fails, the AV node can take over at about 40 to 60 beats per minute, and the ventricles can act as a last backup at about 20 to 40.

turns.q: why does the AV node delay it?
turns.expect: The AV node delay lets the atria finish contracting and empty into the ventricles before ventricular systole; says this detail is general A&P knowledge beyond their note.
turns.ans:
The AV node delays the signal so the atria can finish contracting and push their blood down into the ventricles before the ventricles squeeze. Without that pause, the two chambers would contract at the same time and the ventricles would get less blood.

The delay happens because the AV node conducts slowly. Its cells are small and connect to each other poorly, and its action potentials depend on slow calcium channels, so the impulse takes about 0.1 seconds to pass through.

It also acts as a gatekeeper. If the atria beat very fast, such as in atrial fibrillation, the slow AV node limits how many of those impulses reach the ventricles, which keeps the heart rate from getting dangerously high.

turns.expect: Adds more detail: atrial depolarization from SA node, ~0.1 s AV delay, bundle of His to right/left bundle branches, Purkinje fibers spreading apex to base; flags additions as beyond their note.
turns.ans:
Here's more detail on the AV node and how it fits the whole conduction system.

Where it sits: The AV node is in the lower part of the interatrial septum, near the opening of the coronary sinus. Electrically, the atria and ventricles are separated by a fibrous skeleton that doesn't conduct, so the AV node is the only normal bridge for the impulse.

Why it's slow (about 0.1 seconds):

Its cells are small and have few gap junctions (mainly connexin 45, versus connexin 43 in the atria and ventricles), so the impulse passes between cells slowly.
Its action potential upstroke depends on slow calcium channels (L-type), not the fast sodium channels used in the atria and ventricles. Slow upstrokes mean slow conduction.
The result is conduction velocity of only about 0.05 m/s, compared with roughly 1 m/s in the atrial muscle and 2 to 4 m/s in the Purkinje fibers.

Why the delay matters:

During the delay, the atria finish contracting and push blood into the ventricles. This 'atrial kick' supplies roughly 20 to 30 percent of ventricular filling at rest, and more during exercise.
The delay also gives the ventricles time to fill before they contract, so the pump works efficiently.

Nervous system control:

The parasympathetic (vagus) nerve releases acetylcholine, which slows AV conduction and lengthens the delay.
The sympathetic system releases norepinephrine, which speeds AV conduction.

The gatekeeper role: In atrial fibrillation, the atria fire chaotically at 300 or more impulses per minute. The AV node's slow, refractory conduction lets only a fraction through, so the ventricles beat at a more controlled rate. Drugs such as beta blockers and certain calcium channel blockers slow AV conduction on purpose for rate control.

After the AV node: The impulse moves quickly through the bundle of His, the left and right bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers. This fast spread is why the ventricles contract almost together, from the apex upward.

If you'd like, I can explain the PR interval on an ECG, which shows this delay as a measurable segment.

turns.expect: Ego mediates between id demands and reality using the reality principle and defense mechanisms, per their Freud note.
turns.ans:
In Freud's model, the ego is the rational part of the mind that balances the id's urges, the superego's moral rules and the demands of the real world.

It runs on the reality principle. Where the id wants immediate pleasure, the ego works out what is possible and safe, and can delay gratification until the right time.
It mediates between the id and the superego, so a wish can be expressed in a form that is acceptable.
When anxiety builds up from conflicts between these forces, the ego uses defense mechanisms such as repression, rationalization, displacement and sublimation to reduce it. These work unconsciously.
It develops in early childhood as the person learns what the world allows and how to meet needs in socially acceptable ways.

For nursing, the main idea is that a patient's coping often reflects how well their ego is managing these pressures.

turns.q: why does it need defense mechanisms?
turns.expect: Because the ego must manage anxiety arising from conflict between id impulses, superego demands and reality; defense mechanisms reduce that anxiety unconsciously.
turns.ans:
The ego uses defense mechanisms to manage anxiety. It sits between three pressures: the id's urges, the superego's rules, and what's realistic. When those clash, the tension feels like anxiety, and the ego needs a way to reduce it without ignoring reality completely.

Defense mechanisms do this by working unconsciously to distort or block the threatening thought or impulse:

Repression pushes a painful thought out of awareness.
Projection puts an unacceptable feeling onto someone else.
Displacement redirects an emotion to a safer target.
Rationalization creates a logical-sounding excuse.
Sublimation channels the urge into an acceptable activity.

They help in the short term by keeping anxiety manageable, so the person can keep functioning. Some are healthier than others, though. Sublimation is generally considered adaptive, while heavy reliance on projection or repression can distort how a person sees reality.

For nursing, this means a patient's defenses are normal coping. Your job is to understand what they're protecting against, not to judge them for it.

turns.expect: Patient unconsciously redirects feelings about someone from their past onto the nurse (their note).
turns.ans:
Transference is when a person unconsciously redirects feelings, expectations or attitudes they had toward someone significant in their past onto someone in the present. In a nursing relationship, the patient might treat the nurse like a parent, an old partner or a authority figure from their history.

It can be positive (warmth, trust, wanting approval) or negative (anger, distrust, feeling judged), and the patient often isn't aware it's happening.

For nurses, the key points are:

Recognize it: the patient's reaction seems bigger or different than the situation calls for.
Don't take it personally, and don't reciprocate or act on it.
Keep the relationship professional and therapeutic, with clear boundaries.
Use it to understand the patient better, and talk it through with a supervisor if it's affecting you.

It's the opposite of countertransference, which is the nurse's own emotional reaction to the patient, based on the nurse's past relationships.

turns.expect: Example: a patient treats an older female nurse with hostility because she reminds him of his critical mother.
turns.ans:
Here's a nursing example: A patient, Mr. Lewis, is in the hospital after surgery. Each time the nurse comes in to check his vitals, he gets short with her and says she never listens, just like his older sister used to. The nurse didn't do anything to upset him. His reaction comes from the old sibling relationship, so he's redirecting those feelings onto her.

The nurse can recognize the pattern because his anger is much bigger than the situation calls for. She stays calm, doesn't take it personally, keeps her tone professional, and responds to his actual needs. If it keeps happening, she can talk it over with her supervisor.

turns.q: how is that different from countertransference?
turns.expect: Transference is the patient's feelings onto the nurse; countertransference is the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient from the nurse's own past; nurse should recognize it and seek supervision.
turns.ans:
The difference is whose past is shaping the feelings, and who is having them.

Transference happens with the patient. They unconsciously redirect feelings from someone important in their past (a parent, sibling or former partner) onto the nurse.
Countertransference happens with the nurse. It's the nurse's own emotional reaction to the patient, shaped by the nurse's past relationships.

For example, if a patient keeps treating you like their critical father, that's transference. If you feel unusually irritated by a patient who reminds you of your own demanding father, that's countertransference.

Both are normal, and both need to be handled professionally. Nurses should notice these reactions, keep their boundaries clear, and talk them through with a supervisor if they're affecting care.

turns.expect: Albert Ellis's therapy: identify and dispute irrational beliefs (musts, shoulds) and replace with rational ones using the ABC model (Activating event, Belief, Consequence).
turns.ans:
REBT (rational-emotive behavior therapy) is a form of cognitive behavioral therapy developed by Albert Ellis. Its core idea is that we're upset less by events themselves than by our beliefs about them, especially rigid demands like "I must," "they should," or "it's awful."

It uses the ABC model:

A (Activating event): what happened
B (Belief): what you tell yourself about it, often irrational
C (Consequence): the emotion and behavior that follow

In practice, the therapist or client also disputes the irrational belief (D) by asking whether it's realistic, logical and helpful, then builds a more effective, rational belief (E). The aim is a healthier feeling and behavior, such as concern or disappointment instead of rage or panic.

REBT targets common irrational beliefs: demanding that things or people be a certain way, catastrophizing, low frustration tolerance, and rating yourself as a whole person based on one event. It replaces them with flexible preferences, like "I'd like this to go well, and if it doesn't, it's bad but I can cope."

For example, failing a quiz (A) may lead to "I must pass, so I'm a failure" (B), which causes despair (C). Disputing that belief might lead to "I wanted a better result, so I'll review what went wrong" (E).

turns.expect: Example ABC: A = failing a quiz, B = 'I must never fail, I'm stupid', C = depression/avoiding studying; disputing B leads to a rational belief and healthier consequence.
turns.ans:
Here's a quick example:

A (Activating event): You get 12/20 on a quiz.
B (Belief): "I must do well on every quiz. This proves I'm bad at nursing."
C (Consequence): You feel hopeless and avoid opening your notes.

To dispute the belief, ask: Is it true that I must get every quiz right? Does thinking this way help me study? Would I say this to a friend?

E (Effective, rational belief): "I wanted a better mark, so I'll find the questions I missed and go over them."

The feeling shifts from despair to disappointment, and you take a useful step.

turns.q: how would a nurse use that
turns.expect: Nurse helps the patient spot 'musts/shoulds', question the evidence, and reframe to a rational belief, e.g. via questioning during therapeutic communication.
turns.ans:
A nurse uses REBT ideas mainly in two ways.

With patients: Nurses notice when a patient's distress comes from rigid beliefs, like "I must never need help" or "I'm a failure if I can't go home today." Nurses can gently ask what the patient is telling themselves about the situation, help them see whether that belief is realistic, and encourage more flexible thinking, such as "I'd like to manage this on my own, and it's okay to accept support." This supports coping, adherence to treatment and mental health recovery.
For themselves: Nursing is demanding, so nurses use the same ABC model on their own stress. For example, a rough shift (A) can lead to "I must be perfect or I'm useless" (B), which causes burnout (C). Disputing that belief helps them respond with more balance and keep caring for patients.

In your Psychiatric Nursing course, this links well with the therapeutic relationship and Peplau's phases, since the nurse's role is to guide the patient toward healthier beliefs in a safe, professional way.

turns.expect: Uses their note: MAIN long-term causes (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism) and the spark, assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, June 1914.
turns.ans:
WWI started because a political assassination set off a chain of alliance commitments, and the tensions behind it had been building for years.

The spark: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to a secret Serbian group. Austria-Hungary blamed the Serbian government.

The chain reaction:

Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum in late July, and Germany backed it with a "blank cheque" of support.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on July 28.
Russia, allied to Serbia, began mobilizing its army.
Germany declared war on Russia (August 1) and France (August 3), then invaded neutral Belgium on the way to France.
Britain declared war on Germany on August 4, mainly because of the violation of Belgian neutrality.

The underlying causes:

Militarism: Major powers built up large armies and navies, especially an Anglo-German naval race.
Alliances: Europe was split into the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, though Italy stayed out at first), so a local conflict could pull in everyone.
Imperialism: Rivalry over colonies and markets created mistrust between powers.
Nationalism: Ethnic and national movements in the Balkans, especially Serbian and Slavic nationalism against Austria-Hungary, made the region unstable.

In short, the assassination was the trigger, but the alliance system turned a regional crisis into a continental war.

turns.q: how did the alliances make it worse
turns.expect: Alliances (Triple Entente vs Triple Alliance / Central Powers) turned a regional Austria-Serbia conflict into a continental war as allies were pulled in; notes alliance details are general knowledge beyond their note.
turns.ans:
Alliances turned a regional conflict into a war between most of Europe. Before 1914, Europe was divided into two blocs: the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, with Italy initially staying out).

Encouraging a hard line: Germany's "blank cheque" told Austria-Hungary it had German backing, so Vienna was willing to take a harsh stance against Serbia and risk war.
Pulling in more countries: When Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia, Russia mobilized to defend its Slavic ally. Germany then declared war on Russia (August 1) and on France (August 3), since France was Russia's ally.
Mobilization timetables: Armies were planned to move quickly, so mobilizing one country pushed others to mobilize too. This made it hard to stop the escalation once it started.
Germany's invasion of Belgium: Germany's war plan required a fast attack on France through neutral Belgium. Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality and was tied to France through the Entente, so it declared war on Germany on August 4.

In short, the alliances meant that a local crisis in the Balkans quickly became a continental war, and then a world war as the conflict spread to colonies and other regions.

turns.expect: Moral component / conscience holding internalized parental and societal standards, producing guilt; ties to their Freud note.
turns.ans:
The superego is the moral part of Freud's model of personality. It holds the internalized rules, values and standards we absorb from parents, teachers and society, and it judges our thoughts and actions as right or wrong.

Where it comes from: It forms in early childhood, as children take in their parents' rules and then society's expectations.
What it does: It pushes against the id's urge for immediate gratification with moral demands. It also includes the ego ideal, the picture of who you want to be, which can make you feel proud when you meet it.
How it shows up: When you break a rule you believe in, the superego produces guilt. A simple example: you want to take the last cookie you were told to leave alone, and the feeling that it would be wrong is the superego at work.
Its place in the structure: The id wants pleasure, the superego demands morality, and the ego, which works on the reality principle, mediates between them using defense mechanisms.

turns.q: how does it fight with the id
turns.expect: Id wants immediate gratification, superego demands moral perfection; the ego mediates between them and reality.
turns.ans:
The superego fights the id by putting moral limits on its urges. The id wants whatever feels good right now, and the superego answers with "that's wrong" or "you should not."

Here's how the struggle usually plays out:

The id pushes: It wants immediate satisfaction, such as lashing out at someone who annoyed you.
The superego pushes back: It judges that impulse against your internalized rules and values, and if you act on it anyway, it produces guilt. Its ego ideal can also make you feel ashamed for falling short of who you want to be.
The ego negotiates: It works on the reality principle, so it looks for a compromise that gets some of what the id wants without breaking the superego's rules. That might mean venting by going for a run instead of snapping at someone, which is sublimation.

So the superego doesn't simply shut the id down. It sets the moral boundaries, and the ego finds a workable path between them.

turns.expect: Example: id wants to take a coworker's lunch, superego says stealing is wrong and induces guilt, ego finds a realistic option like buying food.
turns.ans:
Here's a quick everyday example of the superego at work:

The situation: You're at a friend's place and see a "do not eat" label on the leftover pie your roommate saved for tomorrow.
The id: It wants that slice right now, because it's sweet and you're hungry.
The superego: It replies, "That's not yours to take, and you know it's wrong." If you ate it anyway, the guilt you'd feel afterward is the superego's doing.
The ego: It finds a compromise, such as asking your roommate if you can have a slice, so you get the pie without breaking the rule.

So the superego sets the moral limit, and the ego figures out how to meet the id's need within it.

turns.q: what does the SA node do
turns.expect: It is the heart's natural pacemaker, starting each impulse that travels to the AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibers (their note and Heart deck).
turns.ans:
The SA node (sinoatrial node) is the heart's natural pacemaker. It's a small cluster of specialized cells in the upper wall of the right atrium that generates electrical impulses on its own, without needing nerve signals.

Each impulse spreads across both atria, making them contract and push blood into the ventricles.
The signal then reaches the AV node, which briefly delays it so the atria can finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
The impulse then travels down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, causing the ventricles to contract and eject blood.

The SA node sets the rhythm. Its firing rate, about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest, is adjusted by the autonomic nervous system: sympathetic activity speeds it up and parasympathetic activity (the vagus nerve) slows it down.

turns.expect: From general knowledge: other pacemaker sites take over at slower intrinsic rates (AV node ~40-60 bpm, ventricles ~20-40), may need an artificial pacemaker; flagged as not in their notes.
turns.ans:
If the SA node fails, the heart doesn't stop, because other tissue takes over pacing. The AV node (and the bundle of His) can fire on its own, usually at a slower rate of about 40 to 60 beats a minute. If the AV node also fails, the Purkinje fibers can still pace the ventricles, but more slowly, around 20 to 40 beats a minute.

A slower rhythm can cause dizziness, fatigue, shortness of breath, or fainting, because the body gets less blood flow.
When the heart's own pacemaker is too slow or unreliable, doctors often fit an artificial pacemaker, a small device that sends the electrical impulse when needed.

This is a good one to remember for your A&P lab, since it shows why the conduction pathway has backups.

turns.expect: From their MAIN note it is one of the four causes; explains it as the build-up of armies/navies and glorification of military power, e.g. the Anglo-German naval race (latter is general knowledge).
turns.ans:
Militarism is the belief that a nation should build up and prepare its armed forces, and that military strength is the main way to protect or advance its interests. It usually shows up as:

Large standing armies and heavy military spending
Arms races, where rival countries keep outbuilding each other
Military leaders and values having a strong say in government and public life
Treating war as a normal, acceptable tool of foreign policy

Before 1914, the European powers competed fiercely in armies and navies, such as the naval race between Britain and Germany, and their war plans relied on quick mobilization. That kind of readiness made a local crisis much easier to escalate into a continental war.

turns.expect: Competition among European powers for colonies and resources (e.g. in Africa) creating rivalry; one of the MAIN causes in their note.
turns.ans: Imperialism is when a country extends its power over other lands and peoples, usually by taking colonies, controlling their resources and markets, or dominating them politically and economically without formally annexing them. Before 1914, European powers competed fiercely for colonies in Africa and Asia, and that rivalry for territory and influence heightened tensions between them. In your WWI notes, it's the I in MAIN, alongside Militarism, Alliances and Nationalism, all of which helped turn the assassination in Sarajevo into a wider war.

turns.expect: Says historians debate this; gives a balanced view (e.g. alliances turned a local crisis into a world war) and suggests making an argued case for their History Essay due Nov 29.
turns.ans:
Historians still argue about this, but I'd say alliances mattered most. They turned a local crisis into a continental war. Austria-Hungary's conflict with Serbia after the assassination in Sarajevo drew in Russia, which backed Serbia, and then Germany, which backed Austria-Hungary. France was tied to Russia, and Britain was drawn in after Germany invaded Belgium.

The other three set the conditions for that to happen. Militarism made quick mobilization plans seem necessary, nationalism made Serbia and Austria-Hungary more willing to clash, and imperialism fed rivalry between the great powers. But without the alliance system, the assassination would most likely have stayed a regional dispute.

turns.expect: Hildegard Peplau's interpersonal relations theory: the nurse-patient relationship moves through orientation, working (identification, exploitation), and termination/resolution phases, per their Therapeutic relationship note.
turns.ans:
Peplau's theory, from Hildegard Peplau's 1952 book *Interpersonal Relations in Nursing*, sees the nurse-patient relationship as a therapeutic, goal-directed process. Nursing care works through the relationship itself, and both the nurse and the patient learn and grow through it.

The relationship moves through four phases:

Orientation: the patient identifies a need, and the nurse and patient meet and build trust.
Identification: the patient accepts help and feels connected to the nurse.
Exploitation: the patient uses the available services and resources to meet their needs.
Resolution: the patient's needs are met, and the relationship ends.

Peplau also described the nurse's roles as stranger, resource person, teacher, leader, surrogate, and counselor, depending on what the patient needs at each point.

Your note groups the middle phases together as orientation, working, and termination, which is a simpler version of the same model.

turns.expect: Simple version: get to know each other and set goals, work on the problems together, then wrap up and say goodbye.
turns.ans:
Peplau's idea is that a nurse and patient build a helping relationship, and that relationship is the main tool of care.

The relationship goes through three steps:

Orientation: The patient has a need, and they meet and start to trust each other.
Working: The patient accepts help, uses the resources available, and they work on the problem together.
Termination: The patient's needs are met, and the relationship ends.

Your notes use these three steps, so you can remember it that way for class.

turns.expect: Ventricles relax and fill with blood, per their Cardiac cycle note.
turns.ans:
Diastole is the relaxation and filling phase of the cardiac cycle. The ventricles relax, their pressure drops, and blood flows into them from the atria.

The aortic and pulmonary valves close, so no blood leaves the heart.
The tricuspid and mitral valves open, letting blood move from the atria into the ventricles.
Most of the filling happens passively in early diastole, as blood flows down the pressure gradient.
Near the end, the atria contract (atrial systole) to top up the ventricles.

Diastole is the longer part of the cycle at a normal resting heart rate, which gives the ventricles time to fill before the next systole (contraction and ejection).

turns.expect: Adequate filling determines how much blood is ejected next beat (preload/stroke volume) and coronary arteries perfuse mostly during diastole; flags as general knowledge.
turns.ans:
Filling matters because the ventricles can only pump out the blood they hold.

Stroke volume: The more blood the ventricles fill with during diastole, the more they stretch, and by the Frank-Starling mechanism they contract more forcefully. This means more blood is ejected with each beat.
Coronary blood flow: The heart muscle gets most of its own blood supply during diastole. During systole the contracting muscle squeezes the coronary arteries, so the heart is mainly perfused when it relaxes.
Heart rate limits: Diastole is the part of the cycle that shortens when the heart beats faster. If the heart rate gets too high, the ventricles have less time to fill, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall.

turns.expect: Id seeks immediate gratification of instinctual drives, per their Freud note.
turns.ans:
The pleasure principle is Freud's idea that the mind's primitive drive is to seek immediate gratification and avoid pain or tension. The id runs on it, wanting hunger, sexual, and other urges satisfied right away, with no regard for consequences.

It works alongside the reality principle, which belongs to the ego. The ego holds off on gratification when needed so the person can act realistically and safely. In your Freud notes, the id follows the pleasure principle, and the ego follows the reality principle.

turns.expect: Simple analogy: the id is like a toddler who wants candy NOW and doesn't care about rules.
turns.ans:
Okay, here's the simple version. Freud thought your brain has a part that just wants stuff right now, like when you're hungry or tired, and it doesn't care whether it's a good idea. That's the pleasure principle. Think of a toddler who wants the cookie the second they see it.

Then there's the part of you that says, wait, we can have that cookie after dinner. That's the reality principle. It keeps you out of trouble and helps you get along with people.

So one part wants fun now, and the other part plans so you can get what you want without a mess.

turns.expect: It lets emotion out on a safer target than the real source (angry at boss, yells at dog), avoiding the risk of confronting the source, per their note.
turns.ans:
Displacement protects you by moving a feeling away from a target that feels dangerous and onto one that feels safe.

It avoids a risky confrontation. You can't yell at your boss without risking your job, so the anger goes out at someone who can't punish you, like a dog, a sibling or a pillow.
It lowers anxiety fast. Letting the emotion out somewhere, even at the wrong target, brings tension down quickly.
It keeps your self-image intact. You don't have to admit you're afraid of the real source, so you can feel in control.

The cost is that the real problem stays unresolved, and the safer target often gets hurt or confused by feelings that weren't really about them. It's a defense mechanism because it works in the moment but doesn't address what's underneath.

turns.expect: Explains it reduces anxiety short-term but can harm relationships; less adaptive than sublimation; nurses should help patients identify the true source of feelings.
turns.ans:
It depends on how often it happens and what it costs you.

Occasionally, it's normal. Everyone redirects a bit of feeling now and then, like snapping at a sibling after a bad day at work. It's usually harmless if you notice it and the target isn't hurt much.
Regularly, it's unhealthy. The real problem never gets addressed, so the stress keeps building. The people nearby, often those who are safe to be angry at, end up absorbing feelings that weren't about them, and relationships get strained.

Healthier options include naming the real feeling ("I'm angry at my boss, not my partner"), talking to the actual person when it's safe, or doing something physical like a walk to bring the tension down. Writing it out in a journal can also help you see what's underneath.

turns.q: explain nationalism as a cause of WWI
turns.expect: Intense pride/loyalty to one's nation and ethnic groups seeking independence, e.g. Serbian nationalism in the Balkans; MAIN cause per their note, details from general knowledge.
turns.ans:
Nationalism was a major cause of WWI because it made many people in Europe fiercely loyal to their own nation and suspicious of others, which raised tensions across the continent.

Rival national movements in the Balkans: Serbian nationalists wanted to unite South Slavs and free them from Austro-Hungarian rule, while Russia backed Pan-Slavism, the idea of uniting Slavic peoples. Austria-Hungary, a multi-ethnic empire, saw these movements as a threat to its survival. The Balkans became known as the "powder keg of Europe."
Ethnic tensions inside empires: Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire contained many nationalities that wanted independence or more autonomy, so their rulers felt pressure to act firmly.
Unfinished grievances: France wanted to recover Alsace-Lorraine, which Germany had taken after the Franco-Prussian War in 1871. This desire for revenge kept Franco-German relations hostile.
Pride and competition: Growing national pride in Germany, Britain, France and Russia encouraged arms races and imperial rivalry, and made leaders reluctant to back down.

Nationalism also fed the spark. In June 1914, Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on July 28, 1914. Because of the alliance system, Russia, Germany, France and Britain were quickly drawn in.

turns.q: how does that connect to Franz Ferdinand
turns.expect: He was assassinated in Sarajevo (June 1914) by a Bosnian Serb nationalist (Gavrilo Princip), linking nationalism to the spark in their note.
turns.ans:
Franz Ferdinand was heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his assassination was the spark that lit the war. On June 28, 1914, in Sarajevo, Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist, shot him. Princip wanted Bosnia freed from Austro-Hungarian rule and joined to Serbia, so the killing was driven by South Slav nationalism.

The nationalist tensions in the Balkans then pulled in the great powers:

Austria-Hungary blamed the Serbian government for the plot and sent it a harsh ultimatum. It declared war on Serbia on July 28, 1914.
Russia backed Serbia as a fellow Slavic state, so it began mobilizing its army.
Germany backed Austria-Hungary, its ally, and declared war on Russia and then France.
Britain entered after Germany invaded Belgium.

So nationalism caused the crisis, and the alliance system turned one assassination into a continent-wide war.

turns.expect: Part of the conduction path between the AV node and Purkinje fibers in their note; conducts the impulse into the interventricular septum.
turns.ans: The bundle of His (also called the atrioventricular bundle) is a bundle of specialized heart muscle fibers that carries electrical impulses from the AV node down into the ventricles. It runs through the interventricular septum and splits into the left and right bundle branches, which lead to the Purkinje fibers. Those fibers spread the impulse through the ventricle walls so they contract together and push blood out. The pathway runs SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.

turns.expect: Last part of the pathway in their note; spread the impulse rapidly through the ventricular walls so ventricles contract (systole).
turns.ans:
Purkinje fibers are the last part of the heart's conduction system. They're specialized fibers that spread out through the ventricle walls, starting from the bundle branches. Once the impulse reaches them, it spreads quickly through the ventricle muscle, so the ventricles contract together and push blood out to the lungs and body.

The full pathway is SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, then Purkinje fibers.

turns.q: a patient blames others for his anger, which defense mechanism?
turns.expect: Projection: attributing his own unacceptable feelings to others, per their Defense mechanisms note.
turns.ans: This is projection. The patient attributes his own unacceptable anger to other people, so the anger feels like someone else's fault instead of his own. It's a defense mechanism because it keeps painful feelings out of awareness. A nurse might notice it when the patient repeatedly says others are making him angry while he doesn't see his own part in it.

turns.expect: Displacement redirects emotion to a safer target while still owning the feeling; projection denies the feeling is his and attributes it to others.
turns.ans:
Good question, because the two look alike. In displacement, the feeling is real and it's aimed at the wrong target. Someone is angry at the boss but yells at the dog, since the boss is too risky to confront. In projection, the feeling is the person's own unacceptable feeling, and they pin it on someone else, like the patient who blames others for his anger and doesn't see it as his own.

For your patient, the clue is that he insists others are making him angry, which is about owning the feeling, so projection fits. If he were angry at one person and taking it out on someone safer, that would be displacement.

turns.q: patient got yelled at by her doctor then snaps at the nurse. what is that
turns.expect: Displacement: redirecting emotion to a safer target (their note's boss/dog example).
turns.ans:
This is displacement, a defense mechanism. The patient's anger started with the doctor, but the doctor felt too powerful or risky to confront, so the feeling was redirected onto a safer target, the nurse.

It's not really about the nurse. A helpful response is to stay calm, avoid taking it personally, and acknowledge the feeling ("It sounds like you're really angry right now"). You can also gently ask what happened with the doctor, and set respectful limits on behavior if needed.

turns.expect: Stay calm, don't take it personally, acknowledge the feeling, and use therapeutic communication to explore the real source of anger.
turns.ans:
The nurse should stay calm and avoid taking the anger personally, since the patient is really upset about the doctor.

Acknowledge the feeling: "It sounds like you're really angry right now."
Stay neutral and respectful: Keep your tone steady and don't argue or get defensive.
Gently explore the real source: Ask what happened with the doctor, and listen.
Set limits on behavior, not feelings: "I want to help, and I need us to talk without yelling."
Offer concrete help: Explain the plan of care, answer questions, or arrange for the doctor to clarify things.
Get support if needed: Seek supervision or involve the charge nurse if the patient stays hostile, and document the interaction.

turns.q: pt says he failed the exam because the teacher hates him and the questions were unfair. defense mechanism?
turns.expect: Rationalization (logical-sounding excuses), possibly with elements of projection; their note defines rationalization as making excuses that sound logical.
turns.ans:
The best fit is rationalization. "The questions were unfair" is an excuse that sounds logical, and it protects his self-esteem by putting the failure outside himself.

The "teacher hates him" part can also point to projection, where he attributes his own unacceptable feelings, such as disappointment or shame about failing, onto someone else.

For your case study, you'd name rationalization as the main mechanism and mention projection as a possible second one. Look for how he responds if you gently ask what he thinks went wrong, since that's where a nurse can help him see the pattern.

turns.q: what's the difference between that and projection here
turns.expect: Rationalization justifies the failure with reasonable-sounding excuses; projection would attribute his own feelings (e.g. his hostility) to the teacher.
turns.ans:
The difference is in where the patient puts the blame and why.

Rationalization is about the excuse. He gives a logical-sounding reason for the failure, like "the questions were unfair," so the explanation sounds reasonable even though it isn't the real cause.
Projection is about the feeling. He takes his own unacceptable feelings, such as shame or disappointment, and places them on someone else, like "the teacher hates me." The teacher is the target of what he's feeling inside.

In his case, "the questions were unfair" is rationalization, and "the teacher hates him" is projection. Both protect him from facing his own part in the failure.

For your case study, you can point out that rationalization explains the reason he gives, while projection explains the feeling behind it.

turns.q: a man with aggressive urges becomes a boxer, which mechanism?
turns.expect: Sublimation: channeling urges into socially acceptable activities, per their note and flashcard.
turns.ans: That's sublimation. The man channels his aggressive urges into an acceptable, even admirable, activity. Boxing lets the energy come out in a controlled, socially approved way, which is why sublimation is considered one of the healthier defense mechanisms.

turns.q: a patient can't remember the car accident she was in. what defense?
turns.expect: Repression (pushing painful thoughts out of awareness, from their note); may mention dissociative amnesia as a differential.
turns.ans:
The defense mechanism is repression: the mind pushes a painful or overwhelming memory out of awareness so the person doesn't have to face it.

In nursing terms, keep in mind that repression is a Freudian concept describing how the mind protects itself. If the memory loss is severe, sudden, or tied to the event, it could also be dissociative amnesia, which a provider would need to assess. As the nurse, you'd notice the gap, avoid pressing her for details, and report it to the team.

turns.q: is that the same as denial?
turns.expect: No: repression is unconscious forgetting of a painful memory; denial is refusing to accept a reality that is present (e.g. 'I'm not sick'); denial is not in their notes.
turns.ans:
Not quite. Repression and denial are both defense mechanisms, but they work differently.

Repression pushes a painful memory or thought out of awareness without the person knowing it. The memory is still there, just buried, which is why the patient can't recall the accident.
Denial is refusing to accept a reality that is already present, such as a patient insisting the accident never happened even when the evidence is clear. It is more of a conscious or semi-conscious refusal to acknowledge the facts.

A quick way to remember it: repression is forgetting, denial is refusing to believe.

turns.q: patient tells me 'you're just like my dad, you never listen' - what's happening
turns.expect: Transference: the patient unconsciously redirects feelings about someone from their past (father) onto the nurse.
turns.ans:
That sounds like transference. Your patient is unconsciously redirecting feelings they have about their dad onto you, the nurse. It's about their past relationship, not about you doing anything wrong.

What you can do:

Don't take it personally, and stay calm and non-defensive.
Reflect the feeling back, for example: "It sounds like you feel I'm not listening. Can you tell me more about that?"
Ask what listening looks like to them, so they can say what they need.
Keep your boundaries and your professional role.
Write down what happened and bring it to your clinical supervisor or instructor, since nurses are expected to recognize transference and seek supervision.

If you notice your own strong reaction to the comment, like feeling hurt or wanting to defend yourself, that's countertransference. It's the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient, and it's worth talking through with supervision too.

turns.expect: Stay professional, don't react defensively, gently explore the feelings, maintain boundaries, and discuss with a supervisor/instructor if needed.
turns.ans:
Here's how you can handle it in the moment and afterward:

Stay calm and don't get defensive. The comment is about the patient's past with their dad, so you don't need to prove you're listening.
Reflect the feeling back. For example: "It sounds like you feel I'm not really listening. Can you tell me more about that?"
Ask what listening would look like for them. This turns the comment into something you can work with.
Keep your professional boundaries. Be warm, but don't take on the role of their father or start arguing about whether you listened.
Notice your own reaction. If you feel hurt or want to defend yourself, that's countertransference. Acknowledge it privately and don't let it shape your response.
Document and debrief. Write down what was said and what you did, then bring it to your clinical instructor or supervisor, since this is exactly the kind of situation they want to hear about.

turns.q: I feel really protective of a patient bc she reminds me of my little sister. is that bad
turns.expect: This is countertransference; per their note, nurses must recognize it and seek supervision; it's normal but needs managing to keep boundaries.
turns.ans: Not bad at all. Feeling protective of a patient is a very human response, and it shows you care. It's worth keeping an eye on, though. Your notes call this countertransference: the nurse's emotional reaction to a patient, shaped by the nurse's own past relationships. Noticing it is the first step. Nurses are expected to talk it through with a supervisor or clinical instructor, so you don't have to handle it alone. Would it help to talk through what you're feeling about her?

turns.q: patient keeps saying 'I should be perfect, I must never make mistakes'. which therapy fits
turns.expect: REBT (Albert Ellis): identifies and disputes irrational 'musts/shoulds' and replaces them with rational beliefs.
turns.ans:
Rational-emotive behavior therapy (REBT), developed by Albert Ellis, fits best. It targets demanding beliefs such as "I must" and "I should," which are at the heart of what the patient is saying.

The approach works like this:

Identify the absolute demand ("I must never make mistakes").
Dispute it by asking for evidence, whether it's realistic, and what it costs them (anxiety, avoidance, self-criticism).
Replace it with a flexible, rational belief, such as "I want to do well, and when I make mistakes I can learn from them."

It uses the ABC model: the Activating event, the Belief about it, and the emotional Consequence. Changing the belief changes the consequence.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a close relative and uses similar techniques, so it's also a reasonable answer if the question is broader.

turns.q: break it into ABC for this patient
turns.expect: A = a mistake/event, B = 'I must be perfect' irrational belief, C = anxiety/shame; nurse helps dispute B.
turns.ans:
Here's the ABC model applied to this patient:

A (Activating event): Making a mistake, or facing a task where a mistake is possible, such as a test, a med error, or a patient's question they can't answer right away.
B (Belief): "I must never make mistakes. I should be perfect. If I slip, that proves I'm incompetent." These are the rigid musts and shoulds that REBT targets.
C (Consequence): Intense anxiety, shame or self-criticism after a mistake, avoiding new tasks, overchecking work, or freezing up under pressure.

The key point is that the mistake (A) doesn't directly cause the distress (C). The rigid belief (B) does. So the work is on B.

REBT then adds two steps:

D (Dispute): Ask, "Is it realistic that I'll never make a mistake? Where's the evidence that a mistake makes me a failure? What does this belief cost me?"
E (Effective new belief): "I want to do well, and when I make a mistake I can learn from it and fix it." Changing B to this usually lowers the anxiety and self-criticism in C.

turns.q: first meeting with a psych patient, we set goals and talk confidentiality. which Peplau phase
turns.expect: Orientation phase.
turns.ans: This is the orientation phase, the first of Peplau's three phases (orientation, working, termination). In it you build trust, explain your role and confidentiality, and set goals with the patient. The working phase comes next, when you carry out the plan and work through the patient's issues together. Termination comes at the end, when the relationship and goals are wrapped up.

turns.expect: Working phase (identification and exploitation), where the patient actively works on problems and uses available services.
turns.ans: The next phase is the working phase. This is where you carry out the plan you set together, work through the patient's issues, and use therapeutic communication to support them. Once the goals are met, the relationship moves into termination, where you review progress and close the relationship.

turns.q: patient is being discharged and is sad to say bye to the nurse. which phase
turns.expect: Termination/resolution phase of Peplau's model; nurse addresses feelings of loss and summarizes progress.
turns.ans: This is the termination phase of Peplau's therapeutic relationship. It's the last phase, where the nurse and patient review the progress made, prepare for the end of the relationship, and talk about feelings like sadness about saying goodbye. Feeling sad at discharge is a normal part of this phase, and the nurse can acknowledge it and help the patient move on.

turns.q: a patient's HR is 48 at rest, is that normal per my notes
turns.expect: Below the 60-100 bpm normal range in their note; this is bradycardia (term from general knowledge); could be normal in athletes but should be assessed and reported if symptomatic.
turns.ans:
Not per your notes. Your Cardiac cycle note gives a normal resting heart rate of 60 to 100 bpm, so 48 is below that range. The medical term for this is bradycardia.

A low rate isn't always a problem. Very fit people and some patients on certain medications can run low. Still, a nurse should check the patient's symptoms (dizziness, fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion), their vitals, and their medications, and report the reading to the charge nurse or provider according to your facility's policy.

turns.expect: Above 100 bpm, so tachycardia; assess for causes like fever, pain, anxiety, dehydration.
turns.ans:
115 bpm at rest is above your notes' normal range of 60 to 100 bpm, so it's high. The medical term is tachycardia.

Common causes include pain, fever, anxiety, dehydration, bleeding, certain medications, and heart or thyroid problems. A nurse should check the patient's symptoms (chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, confusion), recheck the vitals, review the medications and recent events, and report the reading to the charge nurse or provider according to your facility's policy.

turns.q: a patient's SA node isn't firing properly. what part of the heart's conduction is affected first
turns.expect: The SA node is the natural pacemaker at the start of the pathway (SA -> AV -> bundle of His -> Purkinje), so impulse initiation is affected; backup pacemakers may take over.
turns.ans:
The SA node is the first part affected. It's the heart's natural pacemaker, so when it doesn't fire, the impulse never starts in the normal place. Because the atria depend on it, atrial depolarization is the first downstream effect: the P wave on an ECG is absent or abnormal, and the atria may contract out of sync.

If the SA node stops working, the AV node usually takes over as the backup pacemaker, at a slower rate of about 40 to 60 bpm. The impulse then still travels through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to the ventricles, but the heart rate drops.

turns.q: patient with strong urge to drink says 'I really want it but I know I shouldn't'. which parts of personality
turns.expect: Id = the urge for immediate gratification, superego = 'I shouldn't' moral conscience, ego = mediates the decision with reality.
turns.ans:
This is Freud's structure of personality at work:

Id: the "I really want it" part. It's the primitive, unconscious drive that seeks immediate gratification, following the pleasure principle.
Superego: the "I know I shouldn't" part. It's the internalized moral conscience, shaped by rules from family and society, and it produces guilt when we go against them.
Ego: the rational part that weighs the two against reality (the reality principle). It's the part that can decide what's actually safe and workable, and it uses defense mechanisms to manage the conflict.

In nursing terms, the patient's struggle is the id and superego pulling against each other, with the ego trying to find a realistic path between them. That's a useful place to start when you explore the urge with them.

turns.expect: Simple version: one part wants it now, one part says it's wrong, and a third part decides what to actually do.
turns.ans:
Sure! Think of your mind like a little team with three players:

Id: the toddler inside you. It wants what it wants right now, like a snack or a drink, and doesn't care about rules.
Superego: the rule-keeper. It learned from parents, teachers and friends that some things are wrong, so it makes you feel guilty when you want to break them.
Ego: the referee in the middle. It looks at what's real and safe, and tries to find a way that works for everyone.

So when the patient says "I really want it but I know I shouldn't," the id is pushing for the drink, the superego is saying no, and the ego is trying to find a middle path. In nursing, that's the moment to help the patient think through a safe choice.

turns.q: a patient cheats on her diet then says 'I deserved it after my stressful week'. defense mechanism?
turns.expect: Rationalization: a logical-sounding excuse, per their note.
turns.ans: This is rationalization. The patient is making an excuse that sounds logical ("I deserved it after my stressful week") so the guilt about breaking the diet feels acceptable. The real reason, wanting the food, is not admitted. It's a common defense mechanism, and in nursing it helps to respond without judging, gently exploring what the stress was like and what they could try next time.

turns.q: a patient who hates his brother insists the brother hates HIM. which one
turns.expect: Projection: attributing his own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
turns.ans: It's projection. The patient's own hatred for his brother feels unacceptable to him, so he attributes it to the brother instead: "he hates me." Projection is a defense mechanism where you place your own unacceptable feelings onto someone else.

turns.expect: Creates a card like 'Patient who hates brother says brother hates him - defense mechanism? / Projection' and offers to add it to the Psych Nursing Terms deck.
turns.ans: You already have a projection card in your Psych Nursing Terms deck: "Define projection" with the answer "Attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else." I didn't add a copy. Would you like a scenario card instead, like "A patient insists his brother hates him, though he hates his brother. Which defense mechanism is this?" with the answer "Projection"?

turns.q: pt angry at wife kicks the wall, defense mech?
turns.expect: Displacement: redirecting emotion to a safer target.
turns.ans: Displacement. The patient is angry at his wife, but she's not a safe target, so the anger is redirected onto a safer one, the wall. It's the same pattern as being angry at your boss and then yelling at the dog. The feeling is real, but it lands somewhere that feels less risky.

turns.q: a nurse feels irritated by a patient who resembles her ex. what's this and what should she do
turns.expect: Countertransference; recognize it and seek supervision, per their Therapeutic relationship note.
turns.ans:
This is countertransference: the nurse's emotional reaction to a patient, shaped by her own past relationships. Here, the patient's resemblance to her ex is bringing up old feelings, so the irritation may have more to do with her history than with anything the patient has done.

What she can do:

Notice the feeling and name it to herself: "This is about my ex, not only this patient."
Check whether it's affecting her care. Is she short with the patient, rushing, or avoiding them? Would she respond differently to someone else?
Keep her care and tone the same as for any other patient, and stick to the plan of care.
Step back briefly if she needs to, such as asking a colleague to take a task, so she doesn't act on the feeling.
Talk it through with a supervisor or preceptor. Nurses are expected to seek supervision when countertransference comes up.
Document only observable facts about the patient's behaviour and care, not her personal reaction.

It's a common and human experience. Recognizing it early is what keeps it from shaping the care.

turns.q: patient keeps telling the nurse she's the only one who understands him, in the working phase. concern?
turns.expect: Possible transference/dependency; nurse maintains boundaries and fosters independence during the working phase, preparing for termination.
turns.ans:
This is worth noticing, but it's usually expected in the working phase and doesn't mean something has gone wrong. When a patient feels you're the only one who understands him, he may be transferring feelings from someone in his past onto you. As trust builds, this is common.

Respond with warmth and empathy, but keep the relationship professional. Don't say or imply that he's special to you, and don't match the "only you" feeling.
Gently explore it. Ask what he feels understood about, and whether he has felt this way toward anyone else.
Encourage other supports, such as family, peers, groups or other staff, so you aren't his only connection.
Check your own reactions. If you feel flattered, protective or more invested than usual, that may be countertransference. Talk it over with your supervisor.
Tell your instructor or clinical supervisor, as your placement requires. Do this sooner if he becomes distressed when you're unavailable, or if he seems increasingly isolated.

turns.q: in my care plan, a patient says 'everyone must like me or I'm worthless'. what intervention from my notes
turns.expect: REBT-based intervention: identify and dispute the irrational 'must' belief and replace it with a rational one (ABC model); relevant to Care Plan 2 due tomorrow (Nov 24).
turns.ans:
Your notes on rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis) fit this well. The goal is to identify and dispute irrational beliefs, especially ones built on "musts" and "shoulds," and replace them with rational ones.

The patient's statement, "everyone must like me or I'm worthless," is the irrational belief. You could work through it with the ABC model:

A (Activating event): a situation that set this off, such as someone not responding warmly.
B (Belief): "Everyone must like me."
C (Consequence): feeling worthless.

For the intervention, help the patient dispute the belief with questions like "Is it realistic that everyone will like me?" and "Where is the evidence that my worth depends on it?" Then help them build a rational replacement, such as "I'd like people to like me, but I don't need everyone's approval, and my worth doesn't depend on it."

turns.q: write that as a nursing intervention
turns.expect: Writes a care-plan style intervention, e.g. 'Assist patient to identify irrational beliefs using the ABC model and challenge them with evidence, replacing them with rational self-statements' with a rationale citing Ellis's REBT.
turns.ans:
Nursing intervention: Cognitive restructuring using the REBT ABC model.

Assess the patient's irrational belief ("Everyone must like me or I'm worthless") and the activating event that triggered it.
Help the patient identify the belief (B) and its consequence (C), such as feeling worthless.
Challenge the belief with guided questions, such as "Is it realistic that everyone will like me?" and "What evidence shows my worth depends on everyone's approval?"
Help the patient build a rational replacement: "I'd like people to like me, but I don't need everyone's approval, and my worth doesn't depend on it."
Encourage the patient to practise the rational belief when a similar event happens, and reassess their self-talk and mood at each visit.

Rationale: REBT targets the "musts" and "shoulds" that drive distress, so disputing and replacing them can reduce feelings of worthlessness.

turns.q: the ventricles are contracting right now - which phase
turns.expect: Systole: ventricles contract and eject blood.
turns.ans: Right now the ventricles are in systole, the contraction phase. They squeeze and push blood out into the lungs and the body. The phase when they relax and fill with blood is called diastole.

turns.q: patient anxious after news of diagnosis, spends all evening cleaning his room. sublimation or displacement?
turns.expect: Likely displacement or another coping behavior; explains sublimation would be channeling urges into a socially valued productive activity, and discusses which fits best with reasoning from their definitions.
turns.ans:
Sublimation is the better fit. Cleaning the room is a socially acceptable, constructive outlet for anxious energy.

Displacement means shifting the feeling onto a different, safer target, such as being angry at your boss and yelling at your dog. The emotion lands on someone or something else. Here, the anxiety isn't aimed at anything new. It's being put into a productive activity, which is what sublimation describes.

In practice, the same behaviour can look like either, so the nurse's question is whether the cleaning helps him feel steadier and still lets him talk about the diagnosis, or whether it's become a way to avoid those feelings altogether. That second pattern is worth noticing and gently exploring.

turns.q: patient with paranoid thoughts accuses staff of wanting to hurt him while he's actually hostile. defense?
turns.expect: Projection: attributing his own hostility to staff.
turns.ans:
The defense mechanism is projection. The patient attributes his own hostile, unacceptable feelings to the staff, so he experiences them as wanting to hurt him.

In practice:

Stay calm, use a non-threatening posture, and keep a safe distance.
Don't argue about whether the staff are dangerous. Acknowledge the fear ("It sounds like you feel very unsafe right now") without agreeing that the staff mean harm.
Set clear, calm limits on hostile behavior.
Watch for escalation and follow your unit's safety protocol, and make sure another staff member is nearby.

turns.expect: Calm, non-confrontational, don't argue with the belief, maintain safety, be consistent and honest; general psych nursing knowledge.
turns.ans:
For a patient with paranoid thoughts who is projecting hostility onto staff, the approach is to stay safe, calm, and consistent rather than debate the belief.

Stay calm and non-threatening. Use a relaxed posture, keep a safe distance, and speak in a low, even voice.
Acknowledge the feeling, not the belief. Say something like "It sounds like you feel very unsafe right now." Don't agree that staff want to hurt him, and don't argue that they don't.
Be honest and predictable. Explain what you're doing and why, keep your word, and use the same staff when possible, since consistency builds trust.
Set clear, calm limits on hostile behavior. State the limit simply, offer choices where you can, and explain the consequence without threatening.
Be transparent about your actions. Avoid whispering or talking about him in front of him, and ask before touching him.
Watch for escalation. Note early signs of agitation (pacing, raised voice, clenched fists) and use de-escalation techniques before a crisis.
Make sure help is nearby. Have another staff member close by and follow your unit's safety protocol.
Document and report. Record the behavior, your interventions, and his response, and share it with the team.

If you're studying this for an exam, remember that the therapeutic goal is to build trust and reduce fear while keeping everyone safe.

turns.q: wats the diff btwn id n ego
turns.expect: Id = unconscious, primitive, immediate gratification, pleasure principle, present at birth; ego = rational mediator between id and reality, reality principle, uses defense mechanisms (their Freud note).
turns.ans:
Great question, these two get mixed up a lot.

Id: the primitive, unconscious part of the mind. It wants immediate gratification of instinctual drives and runs on the pleasure principle. It's there from birth.
Ego: the rational part that mediates between the id and reality. It follows the reality principle and uses defense mechanisms to keep things balanced.
Superego: the moral conscience, made up of internalized rules from parents and society. It causes guilt when you break them.

A handy way to remember it: the id wants, the superego judges, and the ego negotiates between the two.

turns.expect: Superego = moral conscience/internalized standards that judge right and wrong and cause guilt; the ego balances it against the id.
turns.ans: The superego is the moral conscience. It's made up of the rules you absorbed from parents and society, and it's the part that makes you feel guilty when you break them. Think of it as the inner judge, while the id wants and the ego negotiates.

turns.expect: Projection = attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else; displacement = redirecting emotion to a safer target (boss/dog), from their note.
turns.ans:
Projection and displacement are both defense mechanisms, but they handle the feeling differently.

Projection attributes your own unacceptable feeling or impulse to someone else. Example: you're angry at a coworker but insist that they're the angry one.
Displacement keeps the feeling but redirects it from the real target to a safer one. Example: you're angry at your boss but yell at your dog.

In short, projection moves the feeling onto another person, while displacement moves the feeling onto a safer target.

turns.q: give me an example of each
turns.expect: One example per mechanism that clearly shows the distinction, e.g. cheating spouse accusing partner of cheating (projection) vs yelling at kids after a bad day at work (displacement).
turns.ans:
Here's one example of each, using the same situation so the difference is clear:

Projection: You're furious that your study group ran late, but you tell everyone that *they* are the ones being unreasonable and impatient, when really the frustration is yours.
Displacement: You're furious at your instructor for a harsh grade, but you snap at your roommate over a dirty dish instead.

In projection the feeling lands on the wrong person; in displacement it lands on a safer stand-in.
