You're nervous about your own performance in a group project, but every time someone mentions deadlines, you insist that your teammates are the ones who are stressed and disorganized. Which defense mechanism is this: projection or displacement?

turns.expect: Transference: patient's past feelings redirected onto the nurse; countertransference: nurse's emotional reaction to patient from the nurse's own past; nurse must recognize and seek supervision.
turns.ans:
Transference is when a patient unconsciously redirects feelings from someone in their past, such as a parent, onto the nurse. The patient might act toward the nurse as if they were that person.

Countertransference is the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient, shaped by the nurse's own past relationships. The nurse might feel unusually protective, irritated or wanted by a patient for reasons that come from their own history, not the patient's current behaviour.

Transference comes from the patient, and countertransference comes from the nurse. Nurses are expected to notice both and seek supervision when they're affecting the nursing relationship.

turns.expect: Systole: ventricles contract and eject blood; diastole: ventricles relax and fill.
turns.ans:
Systole and diastole are the two phases of one heartbeat.

Systole is the contraction phase. The ventricles squeeze and push blood out to the lungs and the rest of the body.
Diastole is the relaxation phase. The ventricles relax and fill with blood again before the next beat.

In a normal resting heartbeat, diastole lasts longer than systole, which gives the heart time to refill.

turns.expect: Diastole is longer at rest (about two-thirds of the cycle), and shortens as HR rises; flagged as general knowledge.
turns.ans: Diastole is longer. In a normal resting heartbeat, the relaxation and filling phase takes up more of each cycle than the contraction phase, which gives the ventricles time to fill with blood before the next beat.

turns.expect: Repression: unconscious pushing of painful thoughts out of awareness (their note); suppression: conscious, deliberate choice to not think about something (general knowledge, not in notes).
turns.ans:
Both mean keeping unwanted thoughts or feelings out of your mind, but they differ in awareness and intent.

Repression is unconscious. The person isn't aware they're pushing a painful memory or feeling out of mind. In Freud's theory it's a defense mechanism that protects the ego from anxiety.
Suppression is conscious and deliberate. The person knows the thought is there and chooses to set it aside for now, for example deciding not to think about an exam until later.

In short: repression happens without you noticing, and suppression is a choice you make on purpose.

turns.expect: Sublimation channels urges into acceptable/productive activities; displacement redirects emotion to a safer target; both from their notes.
turns.ans:
Sublimation channels an urge into a constructive, socially acceptable activity. Anger becomes boxing or intense exercise, and the energy goes somewhere useful.

Displacement redirects the emotion to a safer target. The feeling stays the same, but it lands on someone or something less threatening. Angry at your boss, you yell at your dog.

The key difference is that sublimation changes the impulse into something productive, while displacement only moves it to a new target.

turns.expect: Sublimation is considered the more mature/adaptive defense.
turns.ans: Sublimation is generally considered the healthier of the two. It takes the same urge and turns it into something productive and socially acceptable, like boxing or intense exercise when you're angry. Displacement just moves the feeling onto a safer target, such as yelling at your dog, so the emotion still comes out without being dealt with. Displacement can work as a short-term release, but it doesn't resolve the underlying feeling and can hurt the people or animals on the receiving end.

turns.expect: Rationalization = logical-sounding excuses; projection = attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
turns.ans:
They're both defense mechanisms, but they protect the ego in different ways.

Rationalization means making up a logical-sounding reason for a behavior or outcome so you don't have to face the real reason. Example: you fail a quiz and say, "The quiz was badly written anyway, so it doesn't count."
Projection means attributing your own unacceptable feelings or traits to someone else. Example: you're angry at a classmate but insist, "They're the one who's angry at me."

A quick way to tell them apart: rationalization explains away your behavior with excuses, while projection pins your unwanted feeling on another person.

turns.expect: SA node: natural pacemaker that starts the impulse; AV node: next in the pathway, receives the impulse and passes it to the bundle of His (with a brief delay, general knowledge).
turns.ans:
The SA node (sinoatrial node) is the heart's natural pacemaker. It sits in the upper right atrium and starts each heartbeat, usually at 60 to 100 bpm at rest. Its impulse spreads across both atria, making them contract.

The AV node (atrioventricular node) sits between the atria and ventricles, at the lower part of the atria. It briefly delays the impulse, about 0.1 seconds, so the atria finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract. From there the signal travels through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to make the ventricles contract.

SA node: sets the rhythm and starts the impulse.
AV node: delays the impulse and passes it to the ventricles.

If the SA node fails, the AV node can take over as a backup pacemaker, but it fires more slowly, at about 40 to 60 bpm.

turns.q: how is REBT different from Freud's approach
turns.expect: REBT (Ellis) focuses on present conscious irrational beliefs and disputing them (ABC); Freud's psychoanalytic model focuses on unconscious id/ego/superego conflicts and defenses.
turns.ans:
The biggest difference is where each approach looks for the cause of distress.

Freud (psychoanalysis) looks to the unconscious and to early childhood. Hidden drives and conflicts between the id, ego and superego are thought to drive symptoms. Therapy uses free association, dream analysis and exploring transference, with the goal of bringing unconscious material into awareness. It is open-ended and often long-term, and the therapist stays fairly neutral.
Albert Ellis (REBT) looks at the beliefs a person holds right now. The core idea is that events don't upset us directly; our interpretation of them does. Using the ABC model (Activating event, Belief, Consequence), the therapist helps the client identify irrational beliefs, such as rigid musts, shoulds and demands, and then actively dispute them and replace them with more rational, flexible ones.

Other differences follow from that:

REBT is short-term, structured and directive. The therapist teaches the model and often assigns homework between sessions.
Freud's method focuses on insight into the past. REBT acknowledges the past but works mainly on changing present thinking.
Freud's therapy is largely exploratory. REBT is more active and educational, and it is goal-focused.

In short, Freud asks, "Where do these feelings come from in my past?" REBT asks, "What am I telling myself about this event, and is that belief helping me?"

turns.q: which would work better for a patient with perfectionism
turns.expect: REBT, since perfectionism involves 'musts/shoulds' that REBT directly disputes; brief reasoning.
turns.ans:
REBT would likely work better for a patient with perfectionism, for a few reasons:

Perfectionism is driven by rigid beliefs. Thoughts like "I must do this flawlessly" or "a mistake means I'm a failure" are the kind of musts and shoulds REBT targets. The ABC model gives the patient and nurse a clear way to examine the belief behind the distress.
It is structured and present-focused. REBT works on how the patient thinks now, which matters because perfectionism shows up in daily decisions, study, work and relationships.
It uses practical homework. Patients can track their demands on themselves and test them, such as deliberately doing a task "good enough" and noticing what actually happens.
Freud's approach can still help in some cases. Exploring where the standards came from, such as demanding parents or a history of conditional approval, may give the patient useful insight. But insight alone often doesn't change the behavior, and the work can be long and open-ended.

Cognitive behavioural therapy, which grew out of ideas like Ellis's, has strong evidence for perfectionism, so REBT's principles fit well there. The best choice still depends on the patient's goals and what they're ready for.

turns.q: alliances vs imperialism as WWI causes
turns.expect: Alliances: mutual defense agreements that pulled nations into war; imperialism: competition for colonies creating rivalry; both from their MAIN note.
turns.ans:
Both were real causes, but they worked differently. Alliances determined how far the war spread, and imperialism supplied much of the rivalry behind it.

Alliances: Europe was split into two blocs, the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy at first). After Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in June 1914, a regional fight between Austria-Hungary and Serbia drew in Russia, Germany, France and then Britain, so a local crisis became a European war.
Imperialism: Countries competed for colonies, markets and resources, especially in Africa and Asia. Germany's late push for colonies set it against Britain and France. Clashes over Morocco in 1905 and 1911 and the Anglo-German naval race increased mistrust, and the Balkans rivalry between Austria-Hungary and Russia was tied to competition for influence in the region.

Imperialism created the tensions, and alliances turned those tensions into a war that drew in the whole continent.

turns.expect: Pleasure principle (id) = immediate gratification; reality principle (ego) = delay/adapt gratification to what reality allows.
turns.ans:
The pleasure principle is the id's drive for immediate gratification: it seeks pleasure and avoids tension or pain, with no regard for consequences or the outside world. The reality principle is the ego's response: it delays gratification until a safe, realistic way to satisfy the urge is available.

For example, a hungry child wants food right now (pleasure principle). An adult who is hungry before dinner waits, or finds a snack that's allowed (reality principle).

Freud saw the shift from one to the other as part of normal development, as the ego matures and learns to deal with the real world.

turns.expect: Orientation: establish trust, roles, goals; working: identification and exploitation, patient actively works on problems with the nurse.
turns.ans:
Orientation phase: The nurse and patient first meet. They build trust, the patient shares their concerns, and together they identify the problem and set goals for the relationship.

Working phase: The patient works on the problems they identified, with the nurse supporting them. This is where the real therapeutic work happens, and where transference and countertransference are most likely to come up.

Termination phase: The relationship ends once the goals are met or the patient no longer needs the nurse. They review progress together and talk through any feelings about ending.

Peplau's original model actually had four phases (orientation, identification, exploitation, resolution), so your note uses a simpler three-phase version.

turns.q: and how is termination different from both
turns.expect: Termination ends the relationship: evaluate goal achievement, address feelings about separation, plan for after discharge.
turns.ans:
Termination is different because it's about ending the relationship well, not about the work itself.

Orientation: the nurse and patient meet, build trust, and agree on the problem and the goals.
Working: the patient works on those problems with the nurse's support. This is where transference and countertransference are most likely to come up.
Termination: the relationship ends once the goals are met or the patient no longer needs the nurse. The pair reviews the progress made, and the patient talks through feelings about the ending, such as loss, sadness, or worry about managing alone. The nurse helps the patient consolidate what they've learned and points them toward other supports if needed.

So orientation sets the direction, working does the change, and termination closes the relationship and makes sure the gains last.

turns.q: whats the diff between ventricles and atria
turns.expect: From general knowledge (their note covers ventricles only): atria are upper receiving chambers, ventricles are lower pumping chambers that eject blood in systole.
turns.ans:
This is a subject question, so here it is directly.

Ventricles are the two lower, thick-walled chambers of the heart. They pump blood out: the left ventricle sends oxygen-rich blood to the body, and the right ventricle sends blood to the lungs.
Atria are the two upper, thin-walled chambers. They receive blood returning to the heart and push it down into the ventricles, filling them before each beat.

In short, atria collect and fill, and ventricles pump out. The thicker ventricle walls are why they can generate the force needed to push blood out of the heart.

turns.q: id vs superego, which is unconscious?
turns.expect: Id is entirely unconscious (their note); superego operates at conscious, preconscious and unconscious levels.
turns.ans:
The id is the more unconscious of the two. Freud saw it as entirely unconscious: it holds primitive urges and runs on the pleasure principle, with no direct contact with reality or logic.

The superego is mostly conscious, through your conscience and sense of right and wrong, but parts of it work unconsciously, such as much of the guilt it produces and the internalized rules you don't consciously recall.

turns.expect: Militarism = build-up and glorification of military power; nationalism = intense loyalty to one's nation/ethnic group; both MAIN causes in their note.
turns.ans:
Militarism and nationalism were both major causes of World War I, but they're different things.

Militarism is the buildup of armed forces and the belief that military strength and readiness for war are good and necessary. Before 1914, Germany and Britain raced to build bigger navies, and the great powers drew up detailed war plans, such as Germany's Schlieffen Plan. Those plans made quick mobilization seem essential, so a crisis could escalate fast.
Nationalism is intense loyalty to one's own nation or ethnic group, and the drive for independence or dominance. In the Balkans, Slavic nationalism (including Serbian nationalism) pushed against Austria-Hungary's control. France wanted revenge for losing Alsace-Lorraine to Germany in 1871.

The two fed each other. Nationalism made the public and leaders willing to back a war, and militarism made war seem winnable and close at hand.

turns.q: which should I make my essay thesis about
turns.expect: Suggests a defensible thesis and points out the History Essay: Causes of WWI is due Nov 29; offers to outline.
turns.ans:
Either one can work. The stronger choice is the one you can defend with the most specific evidence. Ask yourself:

Which one do you have the clearest examples for, such as the naval race, war plans, or the Balkans?
Do you want to argue that one cause mattered more than the other, or that they reinforced each other? Both are valid theses, but they need different evidence.
Which one could you connect to the spark, the assassination in Sarajevo, and show how it turned a crisis into a war?

Once you've picked a direction, try writing your thesis as one sentence that takes a clear position and names the evidence you'll use. If you share your draft thesis, I can tell you whether it's specific enough and where it needs more support.

turns.expect: Repression pushes painful thoughts out of awareness; displacement redirects emotion to a safer target.
turns.ans:
Both are defense mechanisms, but they handle the feeling differently.

Repression pushes a painful thought, memory or feeling out of awareness. The person doesn't consciously know they're holding it, so it can show up indirectly, such as unexplained anxiety or forgetting something important. Example: a patient can't recall a frightening event from childhood.
Displacement keeps the feeling but redirects it from the real target to a safer one. The person is aware of the emotion. Example: someone angry at their boss comes home and yells at the dog.

The simple difference: repression hides the feeling from awareness, while displacement moves the feeling onto a different target.

turns.q: give me a one-page study sheet for A&P quiz 4
turns.expect: Builds a sheet from their Cardiac cycle note and Heart deck (systole/diastole, HR 60-100, conduction pathway); notes the planner doesn't list quiz 4 topics, quiz is Nov 26.
turns.ans:
Study sheet: A&P Quiz 4 (heart and cardiac cycle)

Cardiac cycle

Systole: the ventricles contract and eject blood (into the aorta and pulmonary artery).
Diastole: the ventricles relax and fill with blood. The atria contract near the end of diastole to top them up.
Each full cycle is one heartbeat. Normal resting heart rate is 60-100 bpm.

Conduction pathway (in order)

SA node: the natural pacemaker, in the right atrium. It starts each beat.
Impulse spreads through the atria, which contract.
AV node: slows the signal briefly so the ventricles have time to fill.
Bundle of His, then the right and left bundle branches.
Purkinje fibers: spread the signal through the ventricles, which contract from the bottom up.

Heart sounds and valves

AV valves (tricuspid, mitral) close at the start of systole: the first sound, "lub".
Semilunar valves (aortic, pulmonary) close at the start of diastole: the second sound, "dub".

Key numbers and formulas

Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume (the blood ejected per beat).
Resting cardiac output is about 5 L/min.

Quick self-check

Which node sets the pace, and which node delays the signal?
What happens in systole, and what happens in diastole?
Which valves close to make the "lub" sound?

Tip: say the conduction pathway out loud from SA node to Purkinje fibers until you can do it without looking. If you want, I can quiz you on these one question at a time.

turns.q: add stuff that's not in my notes but probably on it
turns.expect: Adds clearly labeled general-knowledge content like heart chambers/valves, ECG waves (P, QRS, T), stroke volume and cardiac output.
turns.ans:
Here are extra A&P heart topics that often show up on quizzes like this. I can't see the quiz itself, so check them against your lecture slides.

Preload, afterload and contractility

Preload: how stretched the ventricles are at the end of diastole (end-diastolic volume).
Afterload: the pressure the ventricles must push against to eject blood (mainly aortic pressure).
Contractility: how forcefully the heart muscle contracts, independent of stretch.

Frank-Starling law

The more the ventricles fill in diastole, the harder they contract in systole, up to a point. More stretch, more stroke volume.

Stroke volume and ejection fraction

Stroke volume: blood ejected per beat (about 70 mL at rest).
Ejection fraction: stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally about 55-70%.

ECG waves

P wave: atrial depolarization (atria contract).
PR interval: the AV node delay.
QRS complex: ventricular depolarization (ventricles contract).
T wave: ventricular repolarization (ventricles relax).

Circulation

Right heart pumps to the lungs (pulmonary circuit). Left heart pumps to the body (systemic circuit), so the left ventricle has the thickest wall.
Coronary arteries fill mainly during diastole, when the heart muscle is relaxed.

Heart layers

Pericardium (outer sac), epicardium, myocardium (the muscle), endocardium (inner lining).

Blood pressure

Normal resting blood pressure is about 120/80 mmHg: systolic (contraction) over diastolic (relaxation).

If you want, I can quiz you on these one question at a time.

turns.q: how do I remember id ego superego
turns.expect: Memory hook e.g. id = 'I Demand', ego = referee/'Even Out', superego = 'Super-good' conscience; consistent with their note.
turns.ans:
Use a three-step chain: I want, I can, I should.

Id = I want. The impulsive, unconscious part that wants pleasure right now (the pleasure principle). It's there from birth.
Ego = I can. The realistic mediator that balances the id's wants against what's actually possible (the reality principle). It uses defense mechanisms.
Superego = I should. The conscience, made of internalized rules from parents and society. It creates guilt when you break them.

If you picture a toddler grabbing a cookie (id), a parent saying "wait until after dinner" (superego), and the person working out how to get a snack without getting in trouble (ego), the three roles click into place.

turns.q: what about which principle goes with which

Id = pleasure principle. It wants immediate gratification and doesn't care about consequences.
Ego = reality principle. It weighs what the id wants against what's actually possible and safe.
Superego = morality principle. It judges what's right and wrong, and it pushes you toward doing the right thing, sometimes creating guilt.

So the id says "I want it now," the ego says "I can get it in a realistic way," and the superego says "I shouldn't do that."

turns.q: explain the id ego and superego like I'm 12
turns.expect: Kid-friendly analogy: id = wants everything now (pleasure), superego = strict conscience/parent voice, ego = the referee deciding what's realistic; consistent with their note.
turns.ans:
Okay, imagine your mind is like a big house with three roommates who all want different things.

The Id is the toddler roommate. It's the part that wants what it wants right now: food, comfort, fun, no waiting. It's unconscious, which means you don't really see it working. You've had it since you were born.
The Ego is the referee. It looks at what the Id wants and checks it against what's actually possible and safe. It says, "Okay, we can't eat the whole cake right now, but we can have a slice after dinner." The Ego keeps things realistic and uses little tricks, called defense mechanisms, to handle tough feelings.
The Superego is the rule-keeper. It's the voice that learned right and wrong from parents and society, and it's the reason you feel guilty when you do something you think was wrong.

The Id wants fun, the Superego wants you to be good, and the Ego tries to keep everyone happy and get the house running.

turns.expect: Gives fuller version with pleasure principle, reality principle, id present from birth, ego using defense mechanisms, superego as internalized morals.
turns.ans:
Sure, here's more detail on the three parts of Freud's model of personality.

The Id is the oldest part of the mind and the one you're born with. It's primitive and unconscious, and it runs on the pleasure principle: it pushes for immediate satisfaction of basic drives like hunger, comfort, and pleasure, with no concern for consequences or other people. A baby who cries until fed is a good picture of the Id at work.

The Ego develops as a child meets reality. It follows the reality principle, which means it weighs what the Id wants against what is possible and safe, and then finds a workable way forward. The Ego is the part that delays gratification, negotiates between the other two parts, and uses defense mechanisms (such as repression, projection, displacement, rationalization, and sublimation) to manage anxiety.

The Superego forms later, as children absorb the moral rules of their parents and culture. It has two sides: the conscience, which produces guilt when you break a rule you believe in, and the ego ideal, which pulls you toward being the person you want to be. It pushes for perfection and right behavior, often without regard to what is realistic.

In short, the Id wants, the Superego judges, and the Ego balances the two while dealing with the real world. When the Ego is strong and balanced, behavior tends to be healthy. When one part dominates, such as an overly harsh Superego, anxiety and guilt can build up.

Freud's model is historical and hard to test scientifically, but it remains a useful framework in psychiatric nursing for understanding defense mechanisms and how people cope with internal conflict.

turns.q: explain the conduction system like I'm 5
turns.expect: Simple analogy like a spark starting at the SA node (the heart's drummer), passed down a relay of wires (AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers) to make the heart squeeze.
turns.ans:
Your heart has its own electric wiring that tells it when to squeeze. Here's how it works, step by step:

The spark starts at the top. A tiny group of cells called the SA node acts like a little drummer. It sends out a spark that tells the top rooms of the heart (the atria) to squeeze.
The gate waits a moment. The spark reaches the AV node, a gate that pauses it for a split second. This gives the bottom rooms time to fill up with blood.
The signal runs down a path. Past the gate, the spark travels down a path called the bundle of His, then splits into two wires, one for each side.
The bottom rooms squeeze. Little branches called Purkinje fibers spread the spark through the bottom rooms (the ventricles), and they squeeze hard to push blood out to the body and lungs.

Then the heart relaxes and the whole thing starts again with the next spark from the SA node. Every heartbeat is one trip through this wiring.

turns.expect: Simple explanation: a patient treats the nurse like someone from their past because the nurse reminds them of that person.
turns.ans:
Transference is when someone starts feeling about you the way they felt about a different person in their life, often without realizing it.

Imagine someone had a strict teacher who always made them feel small. Years later, a new teacher acts a bit like that, and the student gets annoyed or nervous, even though the new teacher did nothing wrong. Their old feelings got "moved" onto the new person.

In nursing, a patient might feel that a nurse reminds them of a parent, and react to the nurse as if the nurse were that parent. The nurse's job is to notice it, stay calm and kind, and not take it personally.

turns.expect: Simple: the nurse has feelings about the patient because the patient reminds the nurse of someone from the nurse's own life; the nurse should notice and talk to a supervisor.
turns.ans:
Countertransference is the reverse of transference. It's when the nurse starts feeling something toward a patient because of the nurse's own past relationships.

For example, a nurse might feel irritated by a patient who reminds them of a bossy older sibling, or feel overly protective of a patient who reminds them of someone they lost. The feeling comes from the nurse's history, not from anything the patient did.

The nurse's job is to notice the feeling, ask whether it's really about this patient, and keep caring for them fairly. Talking it over with a supervisor or a trusted colleague helps keep the relationship professional.

turns.expect: Simple: it's not what happens to you but what you believe about it that makes you upset; change the 'I must' thoughts and you feel better (A-B-C).
turns.ans:
REBT (rational-emotive behavior therapy) is an idea from Albert Ellis. It says we're often upset less by what happens than by what we tell ourselves about it.

The ABC model:

A: the Activating event (something happens, like a friend not replying to your text)
B: your Belief about it ("She must be mad at me. I can't stand being ignored.")
C: the Consequence (you feel anxious and stop reaching out)

The therapy targets the B. Irrational beliefs are usually rigid "musts" and "shoulds" ("I must be liked," "things should go my way"). You question them and swap them for flexible, rational ones: "I'd like her to reply, but she might just be busy. It doesn't mean I'm unlikable." When the belief changes, the feeling and the reaction usually get milder too.

In one line: change the belief, and the feeling follows.

turns.q: explain WWI causes like I'm in middle school
turns.expect: Simple MAIN explanation with an analogy (e.g. friend groups promising to back each other up), plus the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand as the spark.
turns.ans:
Think of Europe in 1914 as a playground full of kids itching for a fight. Four big reasons got everyone ready to fight:

Militarism: Countries built up huge armies and navies and were proud of them. Germany and Britain were in a race to build bigger battleships, and having a strong military made countries feel they had to use it.
Alliances: Countries made promises to back each other up. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy were one group. Britain, France and Russia were another. So a fight between two countries could pull in everyone.
Imperialism: Europe's countries were grabbing colonies in Africa and Asia for resources and power. They competed with each other, and the rivalry added to the tension.
Nationalism: People were extremely proud of their own country and wanted it to be the strongest. Some groups in the Balkans wanted independence from Austria-Hungary, which made that region a hot spot.

The spark came on June 28, 1914, when a Serbian nationalist shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war. Then the alliances kicked in: Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary, and within about a week, most of Europe was at war.

A quick way to remember the four causes is the word MAIN: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism.

turns.expect: Simple: blaming your own bad feelings on someone else, like saying 'you're mad at me' when you're the one who's mad.
turns.ans:
Projection is a defense mechanism where you take a feeling or thought you find unacceptable in yourself and attribute it to someone else instead. It keeps the feeling out of your awareness.

For example, someone who is secretly jealous of a classmate's success might insist that the classmate is the one being jealous and competitive.

In nursing, watch for patients who blame staff or others for feelings they may actually be struggling with themselves. Your flashcard definition is the same idea: attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else.

turns.expect: Another clear projection example (e.g. someone who wants to cheat accuses their partner of cheating).
turns.ans: Here's another one. Suppose a patient keeps saying the nurses don't care about them, when really they're the one feeling unseen and angry. Projection moves that feeling onto the staff so it feels safer to hold. Your job is to listen for the feeling underneath the accusation, and respond to the patient's need without getting defensive yourself.

turns.q: make systole and diastole make sense to a kid
turns.expect: Squeeze vs relax/fill analogy like squeezing and releasing a water balloon or a pump.
turns.ans:
Think of your heart as a little pump with two halves that take turns.

Systole (SIS-toh-lee) is the squeeze. The heart muscle tightens like your hand squeezing a squishy stress ball, and it pushes blood out to the rest of your body.
Diastole (dy-AS-toh-lee) is the rest. The muscle relaxes, like opening your hand again after the squeeze. The heart fills back up with blood, ready for the next squeeze.

So every heartbeat is one squeeze (systole), then one rest (diastole), over and over. Your heart does this about 60 to 100 times a minute when you're resting. Squeeze, rest, squeeze, rest, all day long!

turns.expect: Turning a 'bad' urge into something good, like being angry and going to play hard at soccer practice.
turns.ans:
Sublimation is a way of handling big feelings or urges by turning them into something healthy and okay.

Imagine you're really angry at your little brother. Hitting him isn't allowed, so you go punch a pillow, run laps, or paint a fierce picture instead. The angry energy is still there, but it comes out in a way that helps you and doesn't hurt anyone.

Psychologists call this a defense mechanism, and they think of it as one of the healthiest ones. Your mind takes something that feels too strong or not allowed and sends it somewhere useful, like sports, art, music, or helping people.

turns.expect: Like a friendship with a goal: meet and set goals (orientation), work on stuff together (working), say goodbye and wrap up (termination).
turns.ans:
Peplau's phases describe how the nurse-patient relationship moves forward, in three steps:

Orientation: The nurse and patient meet, build trust, and figure out the patient's needs and problem together. They agree on goals.
Working: The patient and nurse work toward those goals. The patient explores feelings and changes behaviour, with the nurse's help. This is usually the longest phase.
Termination: The goals are met, the patient is ready to manage on their own, and the relationship ends. The nurse reviews progress and helps the patient deal with any feelings about saying goodbye.

A simple way to remember it: meet, work, then say goodbye.

turns.q: why does the heart have a pacemaker, explain simply
turns.expect: Simple: the SA node is like a built-in drummer keeping the beat so the heart squeezes regularly, about 60-100 times a minute at rest.
turns.ans:
The heart needs its own built-in timer so it can beat steadily without waiting for your brain to tell it to.

The SA node, a small cluster of cells in the right atrium, sends out an electrical signal about 60 to 100 times a minute. That's why it's called the natural pacemaker.
The signal spreads across the atria, making them squeeze and push blood into the ventricles.
It then pauses at the AV node, giving the ventricles time to fill.
Next it travels down the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibers, so the ventricles squeeze together from the bottom up and push blood out.

Without a pacemaker, the parts of the heart wouldn't contract in the right order, and the beat would be uneven or could stop. If the SA node fails, the AV node or Purkinje fibers can take over at a slower rate. Your nerves and hormones then speed the heart up or slow it down to match what your body needs.

turns.expect: Recognizes 'projection': attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
turns.ans:
Projection is a defense mechanism where you attribute your own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else. For example, someone who is angry at themselves might insist that others are angry at them.

It's in your Defense mechanisms note too, alongside repression, displacement, rationalization and sublimation.

turns.expect: Recognizes SA node: the heart's natural pacemaker, starting the impulse to AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers.
turns.ans: Yo! You mean the SA node, short for sinoatrial node. It's a small cluster of specialized cells in the wall of the right atrium, and it's the heart's natural pacemaker. It fires electrical impulses on its own, which starts each heartbeat and sets the normal resting rate of about 60 to 100 beats per minute. The impulse spreads across the atria, then reaches the AV node and travels down through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to make the ventricles contract.

turns.expect: AV node, then bundle of His, then Purkinje fibers.
turns.ans:
After the AV node, the impulse pauses briefly there. That delay lets the atria finish squeezing blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract.

Then it moves in this order:

Bundle of His: a bundle of fibers that carries the signal down the septum between the ventricles.
Left and right bundle branches: they split the signal to each side of the ventricles.
Purkinje fibers: they spread through the ventricle walls and trigger contraction from the bottom (apex) upward.

That upward squeeze pushes blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery. This is systole.

turns.q: superego vs ego idk the diff fr
turns.expect: Ego = rational mediator using reality principle and defenses; superego = moral conscience.
turns.ans:
Good question, they get mixed up a lot! Think of it as three parts of the mind, from Freud:

Id: the primitive, unconscious part that wants what it wants right now (the pleasure principle). It's there from birth.
Ego: the rational part that sits between the id and reality (the reality principle). It uses defense mechanisms to keep things balanced.
Superego: your internalized rules and conscience, picked up from parents and society. It's what causes guilt.

A quick way to remember: the id wants, the superego judges, and the ego negotiates between them.

turns.expect: Ellis's REBT ABC: Activating event, Belief, Consequence.
turns.ans:
The ABC model is the core of Albert Ellis's rational-emotive behavior therapy (REBT). It explains how we get upset:

A, Activating event: what happens, such as a critical comment from a boss.
B, Belief: what you tell yourself about it. REBT focuses on irrational beliefs, often built on "musts" and "shoulds."
C, Consequence: the feeling and behaviour that follows, such as anxiety or avoiding the work.

The A doesn't cause the C directly. The B does. So the therapy helps you identify and dispute the irrational belief and replace it with a rational one.

For example, if your boss criticizes your report (A) and you think "I must never make mistakes, so I'm a failure" (B), you'll likely feel panicked and avoid your next task (C). A more rational belief would be "I'd like to get this right, but a mistake doesn't make me worthless." That usually leads to a calmer, more useful response.

turns.q: ok but y does B matter
turns.expect: Because per REBT the belief, not the event, causes the emotional consequence; disputing irrational beliefs changes the outcome.
turns.ans:
B matters because it's the step you can actually change. The A (the event) is often outside your control: a boss criticizes your report, a exam is hard, a friend cancels. The C (the feeling and reaction) follows from how you interpret the A, and that interpretation is the B.

Two people can face the same activating event and feel very differently. One thinks "this is a useful correction" and feels disappointed but moves on. The other thinks "I must never make mistakes, so I'm a failure" and feels panicked. The event was the same. The belief was different, and the belief drove the consequence.

REBT targets B because irrational beliefs, especially the rigid "musts" and "shoulds," keep producing unhelpful feelings and avoidance over and over. When you dispute the belief and replace it with a more flexible one, the consequence usually gets calmer and more useful.

Notice it. Pay attention to strong feelings toward a patient, such as irritation, over-protectiveness, attraction, or wanting their approval, especially when they don't match the situation.

turns.expect: Recognizes Purkinje fibers: final part of the conduction pathway after the bundle of His.
turns.ans: Purkinje fibers are specialized heart muscle fibers that conduct electrical impulses through the ventricles. They sit in the inner lining of the ventricle walls (the subendocardium) and receive the impulse from the bundle of His and its left and right branches. They spread it quickly into the ventricular muscle, so both ventricles contract together, starting at the apex and moving upward. This pushes blood out efficiently. They conduct faster than most cardiac tissue because they have large cells and few junctions, and they can also take over as a backup pacemaker if the SA and AV nodes fail, though at a slower rate.

turns.q: what's the difference between S1 and S2 heart sounds
turns.expect: Not in their notes; S1 = closure of AV (mitral/tricuspid) valves at start of systole, S2 = closure of semilunar (aortic/pulmonic) valves at start of diastole; general knowledge, linked to their systole/diastole note.
turns.ans:
S1 and S2 are the two normal heart sounds, and they come from the valves closing.

S1 ("lub") is the closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, the AV valves between the atria and ventricles. It marks the start of ventricular systole. It's best heard at the apex, over the lower left chest.
S2 ("dub") is the closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves, the semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles. It marks the end of systole and the start of diastole. It's best heard at the base, over the upper chest.

S1 is usually a little longer and lower in pitch, and S2 is shorter and sharper. S2 is often split slightly during inspiration, when the pulmonic valve closes a bit later than the aortic valve.

turns.expect: General knowledge (not in notes): P wave = atrial depolarization, QRS = ventricular depolarization, T wave = ventricular repolarization; ties to SA node/conduction from their note.
turns.ans:
The ECG (electrocardiogram) records the heart's electrical activity as a series of waves, each one tied to a step of the cardiac cycle:

P wave: atrial depolarization, the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles.
PR interval: the pause while the impulse passes through the AV node, which lets the ventricles fill.
QRS complex: ventricular depolarization, the ventricles contract and eject blood. This is the biggest spike on the trace.
ST segment: the flat stretch after QRS, when the ventricles are contracted.
T wave: ventricular repolarization, the ventricles relax and reset.

The P wave starts at the SA node, the heart's natural pacemaker, and the QRS and T waves follow as the impulse spreads through the ventricles.

turns.q: how does that line up with systole
turns.expect: QRS triggers ventricular contraction (systole begins after QRS), T wave ~ end of systole/ventricular repolarization.
turns.ans:
Systole, the ventricles' contraction and ejection phase, lines up with the middle of the ECG trace:

QRS complex: ventricular depolarization starts, and ventricular systole begins just after it.
ST segment: the ventricles are contracted and ejecting blood. This is the plateau of early systole.
T wave: ventricular repolarization, when the ventricles start to relax. Systole ends around the end of the T wave, and diastole (filling) follows.

The P wave comes before all of this. It marks atrial depolarization, which triggers atrial systole, the short squeeze that tops off the ventricles before they contract.

turns.expect: Not in their notes: CO = HR x stroke volume, about 4-8 L/min at rest; says it's general A&P knowledge.
turns.ans:
Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps out each minute. It's calculated as heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, where stroke volume is the amount of blood ejected from the left ventricle with each beat.

Formula: CO = HR x SV
Normal resting value: about 4 to 8 L/min, typically around 5 L/min in an average adult
Heart rate and stroke volume are the two main factors that change it. Preload (how full the ventricle is at the start of contraction), afterload (the resistance the heart pumps against) and contractility (how strongly the heart squeezes) all affect stroke volume.

In nursing, a drop in cardiac output often shows up as low blood pressure, weak pulses, fatigue, or cool, pale skin.

turns.q: why does that matter for nursing
turns.expect: Low CO causes poor perfusion (hypotension, cool skin, confusion, low urine output); nurses monitor HR, BP, perfusion.
turns.ans:
Cardiac output tells you how well blood is delivering oxygen and nutrients to the body's tissues. If it drops, organs can start to go without enough oxygen, which is why nurses watch for it constantly.

Early warning signs: falling blood pressure, rising heart rate, weak or thready pulses, cool or pale skin, slow capillary refill, and new fatigue or confusion.
Organ effects: less blood reaching the kidneys shows up as low urine output, and poor brain perfusion shows up as restlessness, confusion or drowsiness.
Conditions where it matters: heart failure, heart attack, sepsis, major bleeding, and arrhythmias all reduce cardiac output, and a patient can go into shock if it falls far enough.
Interventions link to its factors: nurses give fluids or diuretics to change preload, control blood pressure to manage afterload, and give medications such as digoxin or inotropes to affect contractility. They also watch heart rate closely because many drugs and arrhythmias change it.

So when you learn the formula, think of it as the thing you're checking at the bedside through blood pressure, pulses, skin and urine output.

turns.expect: Not in their note; Germany's plan to defeat France quickly through Belgium before turning to Russia, which brought Britain into the war; general knowledge for their WWI essay.

The Schlieffen Plan was Germany's military strategy at the start of World War I, drawn up by Alfred von Schlieffen and later revised. Because Germany expected a two-front war against France in the west and Russia in the east, it aimed to defeat France quickly by sweeping through neutral Belgium and around the French fortifications, then turn east to fight Russia before Russia could fully mobilize.

The plan failed. Belgium resisted, Britain entered the war to defend Belgian neutrality, and the advance was stopped at the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914. Both sides then dug into trench warfare on the Western Front.

It fits well with your WWI essay: the alliances and militarism behind it are part of the MAIN causes in your notes.

turns.expect: Not in their note; the diplomatic crisis between the June 28, 1914 assassination and the war's outbreak (Austrian ultimatum to Serbia, mobilizations, declarations of war in late July/early August 1914).
turns.ans:
The July Crisis was the series of diplomatic moves in July 1914 that turned the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (28 June 1914, Sarajevo) into a European war.

5-6 July: Germany gave Austria-Hungary a "blank cheque," promising support whatever Austria did about Serbia.
23 July: Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum with demands it knew Serbia couldn't fully accept.
25 July: Serbia accepted most of the terms but not all, and Russia began preparing its army.
28 July: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
30 July onward: Russia ordered full mobilization, and Germany followed with its own mobilization.
1 to 4 August: Germany declared war on Russia (1 Aug) and France (3 Aug), invaded Belgium (4 Aug), and Britain declared war on Germany (4 Aug).

Each country acted to back its allies, so a local conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia quickly became a general war.

turns.expect: Not in their notes; oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital with approximate ages; general knowledge related to their Freud note.
turns.ans:
Freud's psychosexual stages are five stages of childhood development. In each one, the libido (sexual energy) focuses on a different body area:

Oral (birth to about 1 year): pleasure centres on the mouth, through sucking, biting and feeding.
Anal (about 1 to 3 years): pleasure centres on bladder and bowel control, and toilet training is the main conflict.
Phallic (about 3 to 6 years): pleasure centres on the genitals. Children develop the Oedipus or Electra complex and identify with the same-sex parent.
Latency (about 6 years to puberty): sexual urges are dormant and energy goes into school, friendships and hobbies.
Genital (puberty onward): mature sexual interests develop and are directed toward others.

Freud believed that fixation at a stage, from too much or too little gratification, could shape adult personality traits.

turns.ans:
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a family of talk therapies based on the idea that our thoughts, feelings and behaviors influence each other. A person learns to spot unhelpful or distorted thinking, test whether it's accurate, and change both the thoughts and the behaviors that keep a problem going. It's short-term and goal-focused, and it's used for depression, anxiety, and many other conditions.

Rational-emotive behavior therapy (REBT), developed by Albert Ellis, is one of the original cognitive behavioral approaches, so it's a close relative of CBT rather than a separate idea. The main link is that both say emotional distress comes largely from how we interpret events, and both use structured work to challenge those interpretations.

The differences are mostly in emphasis:

REBT targets irrational beliefs, especially rigid "musts" and "shoulds," and uses the ABC model (Activating event, Belief, Consequence). The therapist directly and actively disputes these beliefs.
CBT (as developed by Aaron Beck) focuses on automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions, such as catastrophizing or mind-reading. The therapist guides the client to examine the evidence through Socratic questioning, working together as a team.

In short, REBT is one of the roots of CBT, and CBT later developed in its own direction with a somewhat gentler, more collaborative style.

turns.expect: Not in notes: tricuspid, pulmonary (pulmonic), mitral (bicuspid), aortic; general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The four heart valves are:

Tricuspid valve: between the right atrium and right ventricle.
Pulmonary valve: between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery, which carries blood to the lungs.
Mitral (bicuspid) valve: between the left atrium and left ventricle.
Aortic valve: between the left ventricle and the aorta, which carries blood to the body.

The two atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) sit between the atria and ventricles. The two semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) sit where blood leaves the ventricles.

turns.expect: Right atrium -> tricuspid -> right ventricle -> pulmonary valve -> lungs -> left atrium -> mitral -> left ventricle -> aortic valve -> aorta.
turns.ans:
Blood moves through the valves in this order:

Tricuspid valve: right atrium to right ventricle.
Pulmonary valve: right ventricle to the pulmonary artery, which carries blood to the lungs.
Mitral valve: left atrium to left ventricle, after the blood returns from the lungs.
Aortic valve: left ventricle to the aorta, which carries blood to the body.

A quick way to remember it: right side first (tricuspid, then pulmonary), then left side (mitral, then aortic).

turns.expect: Not in notes; repeating or paraphrasing the patient's feelings/content back to encourage exploration, with an example; general psych nursing knowledge.
turns.ans:
Reflecting is a therapeutic communication technique where the nurse turns the patient's own words or feelings back to them, as a question or statement, so the patient keeps talking and explores what they mean.

Reflecting content repeats the key words: "You feel you can't manage at home since the surgery?"
Reflecting feelings names the emotion underneath: "It sounds like you're frustrated with waiting."

It encourages the patient to examine their own thoughts and feelings, and it keeps the nurse non-judgmental and focused on the patient rather than offering advice or giving their own opinion.

turns.expect: Not in their notes; lists Erikson's 8 psychosocial stages (trust vs mistrust through integrity vs despair); general knowledge likely relevant to psych nursing.
turns.ans:
Erikson's eight stages of psychosocial development, each a conflict to resolve:

Trust vs. mistrust (infancy, birth to about 1.5 years)
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (early childhood, about 1.5 to 3)
Initiative vs. guilt (preschool, about 3 to 5)
Industry vs. inferiority (school age, about 6 to 11)
Identity vs. role confusion (adolescence, about 12 to 18)
Intimacy vs. isolation (young adulthood, about 19 to 40)
Generativity vs. stagnation (middle adulthood, about 40 to 65)
Integrity vs. despair (late adulthood, about 65 onward)

Successfully resolving a stage builds a strength, such as hope from trust or care from generativity.

turns.expect: Not in their WWI note (which covers causes); 1919 treaty ending WWI, war-guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses for Germany; general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The Treaty of Versailles was the peace treaty signed on June 28, 1919, at the Palace of Versailles near Paris. It ended World War I between Germany and the Allied powers, led by France, Britain and the United States. Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations.

Main terms:

War guilt (Article 231): Germany accepted responsibility for causing the war.
Reparations: Germany had to pay large sums for war damages. The total was set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921.
Territory: Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, gave up land to Poland (including the Polish Corridor), and lost all its overseas colonies.
Military limits: The army was capped at 100,000 men, with no air force or submarines, and the Rhineland was demilitarized.
League of Nations: The treaty created the League, an international body meant to keep peace.

Many Germans saw the treaty as harsh and humiliating, and resentment over it is often linked to the rise of Nazism and the start of World War II.

turns.expect: Not in notes: preload = ventricular stretch/end-diastolic volume, afterload = resistance the ventricle pumps against; general A&P knowledge.
turns.ans:
Preload is how much the ventricle's muscle fibers are stretched at the end of diastole, just before it contracts. It's set mainly by how much blood fills the ventricle (end-diastolic volume), which depends on venous return. More stretch means a stronger contraction, per the Frank-Starling law.

Afterload is the resistance the ventricle has to push against to eject blood. For the left ventricle, it's mainly the pressure in the aorta and the systemic vascular resistance. Higher afterload makes it harder to eject blood, so stroke volume drops.

A quick way to remember it: preload is how full the ventricle is before it squeezes, and afterload is how hard it has to squeeze to get the blood out.

turns.expect: Not in their notes; explains it from general knowledge (biological vulnerability plus stressors trigger illness) and says so.
turns.ans:
The stress-vulnerability model says that a mental disorder appears when an underlying vulnerability meets enough stress. Zubin and Spring developed it in 1977, and it is often used for conditions like schizophrenia.

Vulnerability is a predisposition, such as genetic loading, biological factors, or early-life experiences. It doesn't guarantee illness on its own.
Stress includes life events, relationship conflict, illness, or substance use.
Threshold: symptoms emerge when stress exceeds a person's coping capacity. Higher vulnerability means less stress is needed to trigger symptoms.
Protective factors like coping skills, social support, stable routines, and medication raise the threshold.

For nursing, the model guides you to assess both the person's vulnerabilities and their current stressors, then reduce stress, strengthen coping, and support adherence to treatment.

turns.expect: Not in their notes; performing an act to symbolically cancel an unacceptable thought or action (e.g. giving gifts after an argument).
turns.ans: Undoing is a defense mechanism where a person tries to symbolically cancel out an unacceptable thought, feeling or action by doing something that "makes it right." It often shows up as excessive apologizing, repeating a ritual, or making up for a hurtful act with a gift or kind gesture. Freud linked it to obsessive-compulsive traits, and it can be a way to ease guilt or anxiety without really facing the underlying feeling.

turns.expect: Not in notes; using the structured therapeutic environment of the unit as treatment; general psych nursing knowledge.
turns.ans:
Milieu therapy is a treatment approach in psychiatric and mental health settings where the whole environment is used to promote healing, not just one-on-one sessions.

Structure and routine: Consistent daily schedules, clear rules and predictable limits help patients feel safe.
Therapeutic interaction: Patients practise social skills, communication and conflict resolution with peers and staff in everyday settings.
Group activities: Community meetings, group programs and recreational activities build trust, responsibility and self-esteem.
Staff role: Nurses and other staff model respectful behaviour, support patients, and step in when needed to keep everyone safe.

In nursing, it's often paired with other treatments, and the nurse's consistency is a big part of why it works.

turns.q: what role did the Black Hand play
turns.expect: Not in their note; Serbian nationalist secret society linked to Gavrilo Princip, who assassinated Franz Ferdinand; ties to their note's spark.
turns.ans:
The Black Hand was a secret Serbian nationalist society, founded in 1911 and led by Serbian army officer Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis. Its members included military officers and intelligence men who wanted to unite South Slavic peoples, including those in Austria-Hungary's Bosnia, under Serbia.

Its main role was planning the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. Black Hand members trained the young assassins, including Gavrilo Princip, and smuggled them, along with pistols and bombs, into Bosnia. That killing set off the July Crisis, in which Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, and the alliance system pulled the great powers into World War I.

The group's role was secret and partly known to Serbian officials. The Serbian government later put Apis on trial and executed him in 1917, partly over his plotting against the regent.

turns.q: what's the refractory period in heart muscle
turns.expect: Not in notes; period after depolarization when cardiac muscle can't be re-stimulated, preventing tetany so the heart can refill; general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The refractory period in heart muscle is the time after an action potential during which the cells can't be stimulated again.

Absolute refractory period: The cells can't respond to any stimulus. In ventricular muscle this lasts about 200 to 250 ms, roughly as long as the contraction itself. This stops the heart from going into tetanus, so the chambers can relax and refill between beats.
Relative refractory period: A stronger than normal stimulus can trigger a new action potential. This phase is near the end of repolarization.

Because the absolute refractory period is so long, the heart can't be re-excited during systole, which is why it keeps a steady rhythm.

turns.q: what are the stages of grief
turns.expect: Not in their notes; Kubler-Ross: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance; notes it's general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The five stages of grief, from Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's 1969 book *On Death and Dying*, are:

Denial: refusing to accept that the loss is real, or feeling numb and shocked.
Anger: frustration at the loss, at others, or at yourself.
Bargaining: trying to make a deal or reverse the loss, often with "if only" or "what if" thinking.
Depression: sadness, withdrawal and grief that settles in as the loss becomes real.
Acceptance: coming to terms with the loss and adjusting to life without it.

These stages were first described for people facing their own death. People don't usually move through them in a neat order, and they can come back or overlap. Many grief researchers now see them as common reactions rather than fixed steps.

turns.q: how do defense mechanisms relate to the ego
turns.expect: Per their notes, the ego uses defense mechanisms to protect against anxiety from id/superego/reality conflicts; lists the five from their notes.
turns.ans:
In Freud's structural model, the ego is the part of the mind that balances the id's urges, the superego's moral demands, and the demands of reality. When these pull against each other, the resulting tension produces anxiety.

Defense mechanisms are the ego's tools for managing that anxiety. The ego uses them, mostly outside awareness, to keep painful or unacceptable impulses from taking over. For example:

Repression pushes a painful thought out of awareness.
Projection attributes your own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
Displacement redirects an emotion to a safer target.
Rationalization gives logical-sounding excuses for behavior driven by other motives.
Sublimation channels an urge into an acceptable activity.

Some of these are healthier than others. Sublimation and humor are generally adaptive, while heavy reliance on denial or projection can distort a person's view of reality. In nursing, this is why you might notice a patient's defenses, such as projecting blame onto staff, and respond calmly instead of taking it personally.

turns.q: which one is the most mature
turns.expect: Sublimation.
turns.ans: Sublimation is the most mature of the five. It turns an unacceptable urge into a constructive activity, like channeling anger into intense exercise or a demanding project, so the underlying need is met without harming yourself or others. Projection is generally considered the least mature here, because it distorts how you see other people. Repression, displacement and rationalization fall in between, since they manage anxiety but often at some cost to clear thinking.

turns.expect: Explains e.g. projection or denial are considered more primitive/immature, with general-knowledge caveat.
turns.ans: Projection is the least mature of the five. It's an immature defense because it keeps you from owning your own feelings. Someone who projects might accuse a coworker of being hostile when they're the angry one, so the conflict stays unresolved and their view of other people gets distorted. Repression comes close behind, since it also pushes conflict out of awareness, but it's usually considered more manageable than projection.

turns.q: why should nurses seek supervision for countertransference
turns.expect: Per their note, nurses must recognize it and seek supervision; supervision helps keep objectivity, protect boundaries and patient care.
turns.ans:
Countertransference is the nurse's own emotional reaction to a patient, often rooted in the nurse's past relationships. Because it's hard to see from the inside, nurses seek supervision for a few reasons:

Objectivity: A supervisor can spot when a nurse is treating a patient unfairly, such as being overly protective, irritated, or pulled into a personal role.
Protecting the therapeutic relationship: Unexamined feelings can blur boundaries, lead to over-involvement, or cause a patient to feel judged or rejected.
Safer care: Biased reactions can affect assessments, decisions, and how seriously a patient's concerns are taken.
Self-awareness and wellbeing: Talking through strong feelings with someone else helps the nurse process them and reduces the risk of burnout.

In short, supervision helps the nurse notice the bias, understand where it comes from, and keep the focus on the patient's needs.

turns.expect: Patient works on problems; identification (patient relates to the nurse) and exploitation (makes full use of services); Peplau.
turns.ans:
The working phase is the middle phase of Peplau's therapeutic relationship model, after orientation and before termination. You and the patient work together on the goals and problems you identified at the start. The patient explores feelings, gains insight, and practises new ways of coping, while you use active listening, open questions and steady support. This is usually the longest phase, and it's when transference and countertransference are most likely to come up, so you'd watch for those and talk them through with your supervisor.

Your Therapeutic relationship note lists the three phases as orientation, working and termination.

turns.expect: Example: patient with depression works with the nurse on coping skills and uses group therapy resources.
turns.ans:
Here's a nursing example of the working phase in Peplau's model:

A patient admitted with depression tells you they feel like a failure because they lost their job. In the working phase, you and the patient have already agreed on a goal together: to find ways to manage low mood during the day. You use open questions like "What has helped you get through a hard day before?" and reflect back what they say. The patient starts to notice that short walks lift their mood, so you help them plan one each morning and review how it went at the next session.

While this happens, watch for transference. If the patient starts treating you like a critical parent, that's a sign to talk it through with your supervisor, not to take it personally.

turns.q: why does the heart need a natural pacemaker
turns.expect: The SA node generates regular impulses that coordinate contraction; HR 60-100 at rest, per their note.
turns.ans:
The heart needs a natural pacemaker so that its chambers contract in a steady, coordinated rhythm. Heart muscle can generate its own electrical signals, but without one leading area, different parts would fire at different rates and fall out of sync.

The sinoatrial (SA) node, in the right atrium, fires spontaneously about 60 to 100 times a minute, which sets the heart rate. Its signal spreads across the atria, making them contract and push blood into the ventricles. The signal then pauses at the atrioventricular (AV) node, which gives the ventricles time to fill. It then travels through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, so the ventricles contract together from the bottom up and eject blood efficiently.

Nerves and hormones speed up or slow down the SA node's firing to match what the body needs, but they don't create the beat. If the SA node fails, a backup pacemaker in the AV node or ventricles can take over, though usually at a slower rate.

turns.q: how does it set the rate
turns.expect: Pacemaker cells spontaneously depolarize; autonomic nervous system speeds (sympathetic) or slows (parasympathetic/vagus) the rate; general knowledge.
turns.ans: The SA node sets the rate by firing on its own, spontaneously, about 60 to 100 times a minute. Each firing starts an electrical impulse, so the number of firings per minute is the heart rate. Nerves and hormones then fine-tune it: the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline speed the SA node up during activity or stress, while the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve slows it down at rest. The node's own built-in firing speed is the baseline those signals adjust.

turns.q: explain the B in the ABC model
turns.expect: Belief: the person's interpretation of the activating event; in REBT irrational beliefs (musts, shoulds) drive the consequence.
turns.ans:
In the ABC model from Albert Ellis's rational-emotive behavior therapy, the B stands for Belief.

A (Activating event): what happens, such as a friend cancelling plans.
B (Belief): what you tell yourself about that event, often a rigid "must" or "should" like "She must not like me."
C (Consequence): the feelings and behaviors that follow, such as hurt, anger, or avoiding her.

The key idea is that the event itself doesn't directly cause the consequence. The belief in the middle does. REBT works on the B by identifying irrational beliefs and disputing them, so a more rational belief like "It's disappointing, but she may be busy" leads to a healthier C, such as feeling disappointed and rescheduling.

turns.expect: Rigid, absolute demands (must/should), awfulizing, low frustration tolerance, global self-rating; their note mentions musts and shoulds.
turns.ans:
According to Albert Ellis, a belief is irrational when it is rigid, extreme, or unhelpful. REBT usually points to four patterns:

Rigid demands: "must," "should," or "have to" stated as absolute laws, like "People must always treat me fairly."
Awfulizing: treating a bad event as the worst possible outcome, like "It's the end of the world."
Low frustration tolerance: believing you can't bear something, like "I can't stand this."
Global self-rating: judging your whole self based on one event, like "I'm a failure because I failed one test."

A rational belief is a flexible preference instead. It sounds like "I'd like her to reply, but it isn't necessary." It fits the facts, and it helps you reach your goals.

To test a belief, ask whether there is evidence for it, whether it helps you act toward what you want, and whether it leads to a reasonable feeling. "She must not like me" fails all three, because it's an absolute claim with no evidence behind it.

turns.q: how does the ego handle the id
turns.expect: Mediates using the reality principle, delaying gratification and using defense mechanisms.
turns.ans:
The ego manages the id's urges so they can be expressed safely. It does this in a few ways:

Delaying gratification: It holds back the id's demand for immediate satisfaction until the situation is right (the reality principle).
Redirecting energy: It channels urges into acceptable outlets, such as sublimation, where anger becomes a hard workout.
Using defense mechanisms: When an impulse threatens to cause anxiety, the ego may repress it, displace it onto a safer target, or rationalize it.

The ego also has to balance the id against the superego's moral rules, so it looks for a realistic compromise that satisfies both.

turns.expect: e.g. hungry in class: id wants to eat now, ego waits until break and plans a snack.
turns.ans:
Say you're furious at your boss for piling extra shifts on you. The id wants to yell at them right now. The ego weighs the consequences, since yelling could cost you your job, and steers the anger somewhere safer:

Delaying: You wait until you've calmed down, then raise the issue politely in a meeting.
Redirecting: You go to the gym after work and hit the punching bag hard.
Displacement: You snap at your roommate over a small thing, the anger finds a safer target than the boss.

The ego picks the option that meets the id's need for release without causing trouble with reality.

turns.expect: Transference = redirecting feelings about a past person onto the nurse; projection = attributing one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
turns.ans:
Transference is when a patient unconsciously redirects feelings they had toward someone from their past, such as a parent, onto a person in the present, such as their nurse. A patient who reacts to the nurse as if she were a strict, critical parent is showing transference.

Projection is a defense mechanism in which a person attributes their own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else, so they don't have to own them. A patient who is angry at themselves and insists the nurse is angry with them is projecting.

The main difference is what gets moved. In transference, the feelings belong to an old relationship and get pinned on someone new. In projection, the feeling is the person's own, and they deny it by seeing it in someone else.

turns.expect: Yes; e.g. a patient both reacts to the nurse like a past figure and attributes his own hostility to her; explains.
turns.ans:
Yes, they can happen together, and in practice they often do. Transference is about where the feeling comes from: the patient redirects emotions from an old relationship onto the nurse. Projection is about ownership: the patient attributes their own unacceptable feeling to someone else.

For example, a patient might react to the nurse as if she were their critical father (transference), then insist the nurse thinks they're worthless when the harsh judgment is really the patient's own (projection). The first is an old feeling moved onto a new person. The second is the patient's own feeling denied and seen in someone else.

Spotting both matters for the nurse. Transference signals a need to explore the patient's past relationships, and projection signals a need to gently help the patient recognize the feeling as their own.

turns.expect: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, June 1914 (their note).
turns.ans:
The spark was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist linked to the Young Bosnia movement, shot them during a royal visit to the city.

It set off a chain reaction through the alliance system:

Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and, backed by Germany, sent Serbia an ultimatum on July 23 with demands it knew Serbia would struggle to accept.
Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on July 28.
Russia mobilized to defend Serbia, its Slavic ally. Germany, allied with Austria-Hungary, declared war on Russia on August 1.
France, allied with Russia, was drawn in when Germany declared war on it on August 3. Germany then invaded Belgium to reach France.
Britain declared war on Germany on August 4, mainly because of the invasion of Belgium, which it had guaranteed neutral.

So a regional crisis in the Balkans became a continental war within about five weeks. The assassination was the trigger, but the deeper causes were the militarism, alliances, imperial rivalries and nationalism behind the tensions that made the crisis so dangerous.

turns.q: why did one assassination cause a world war
turns.expect: Because the MAIN tensions (alliances, militarism, imperialism, nationalism) were in place; Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia triggered alliance chain reactions.
turns.ans:
The assassination was the spark, not the fuel. A single murder in Sarajevo caused a world war because Europe in 1914 had several conditions that turned a regional crisis into a continental one.

Alliances tied the great powers together. Austria-Hungary had Germany's backing, while Russia backed Serbia and France had a pact with Russia. Once one country fought, its allies were pulled in.
Germany gave Austria-Hungary a "blank cheque." It promised full support, which encouraged Vienna to take a hard line against Serbia rather than back down.
Mobilization plans were rigid. Russia, France and Germany had detailed railway timetables for moving troops. Mobilizing one side pushed the others to mobilize, so diplomacy had less time to work.
Germany's war plan went through Belgium. The Schlieffen Plan aimed to defeat France quickly by invading through Belgium before turning on Russia. That invasion of a neutral country brought Britain in, since Britain had guaranteed Belgium's neutrality.
Years of tension were already there. Militarism and an arms race, imperial rivalries, Balkan conflicts and nationalism had made the powers suspicious of each other, so each one was ready to see the crisis as a threat to its own position.

So the assassination gave Austria-Hungary an excuse to attack Serbia, and the alliances, war plans and existing rivalries did the rest. Each step looked like a reasonable response to the one before, and within about five weeks, most of Europe was at war.

turns.expect: Orientation (trust, goals), working (identification, exploitation), termination/resolution (end, evaluate).
turns.ans:
Peplau's model of the nurse-patient relationship has three phases in your note:

Orientation: the nurse and patient meet, the patient identifies a need, and they agree on the problem and the goals they'll work toward.
Working: the patient works on the problem with the nurse's help, and this is where transference and countertransference can come up, so the nurse needs to recognize them and seek supervision.
Termination: the relationship ends once the goals are met, and the nurse helps the patient let go and recognize what they've gained.

Some textbooks split Peplau's model into four phases (orientation, identification, exploitation, resolution), with the working phase covering the middle two, so check which version your course uses.
