turns.expect: Summarises Freud's id/ego/superego, defense mechanisms, the therapeutic relationship and REBT.
turns.ans:
Here's a summary of your psych notes:

Freud's structure of personality

Id: the primitive, unconscious part of the mind that seeks immediate gratification of instinctual drives (the pleasure principle). It is present from birth.
Ego: the rational part that mediates between the id and reality (the reality principle). It uses defense mechanisms.
Superego: the moral conscience, made up of internalized rules from parents and society. It causes guilt.

Defense mechanisms

Repression: pushing painful thoughts out of awareness.
Projection: attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
Displacement: redirecting emotion to a safer target (angry at your boss, so you yell at the dog).
Rationalization: making excuses that sound logical.
Sublimation: channeling urges into acceptable activities.

Therapeutic relationship

Transference: the patient unconsciously redirects feelings about someone from their past onto the nurse.
Countertransference: the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient, based on the nurse's own past relationships. Nurses must recognize it and seek supervision.
Peplau's phases: orientation, working, termination.

Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis)

Goal: identify and dispute irrational beliefs (musts and shoulds) and replace them with rational ones.
ABC model: Activating event, Belief, Consequence.

turns.q: what were the causes of ww1
turns.expect: MAIN: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism; spark was Franz Ferdinand's assassination in Sarajevo, June 1914.
turns.ans:
The main causes of World War I are often remembered as MAIN:

Militarism: Major powers built up large armies and navies and expected war to come, which encouraged readiness to fight.
Alliances: Rival blocs, the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy), meant a conflict between two countries could pull in the others.
Imperialism: Competition for colonies and overseas markets created rivalries, especially between Britain, France and Germany.
Nationalism: Intense national pride and ethnic tensions, especially in the Balkans, where Slavic nationalism challenged Austria-Hungary.

The immediate trigger was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and the alliance system then drew in Russia, Germany, France, and Britain within about a month.

turns.expect: Id: unconscious, primitive, seeks immediate gratification (pleasure principle); ego: rational mediator with reality (reality principle).
turns.ans:
Both are parts of Freud's model of personality.

Id: The primitive, unconscious part of the mind. It seeks immediate gratification of basic drives and follows the pleasure principle. It's present from birth.
Ego: The rational part that mediates between the id, the superego, and reality. It follows the reality principle, finding realistic ways to meet needs, and it uses defense mechanisms to manage anxiety.

In short, the id wants what feels good now, and the ego works out how to get it in a way that's realistic and acceptable.

turns.expect: Explains the superego as the moral conscience/internalised standards, noting the note is cut off.
turns.ans: The superego is the third part of Freud's model. It's the moral conscience, made up of internalized rules and values picked up from parents and society. It judges your behaviour against those standards and is what causes guilt when you fall short. Where the id wants what feels good now and the ego finds a realistic way to get it, the superego pushes toward what's right and acceptable, so the ego has to balance all three.

turns.q: how do i memorize defense mechanisms
turns.expect: Suggests mnemonics, examples per mechanism, and spaced repetition with flashcards.
turns.ans:
Defense mechanisms are easiest to remember when you link each one to a clear example and then test yourself on it.

Repression: pushing a painful thought out of your mind. Example: forgetting a upsetting appointment.
Projection: blaming someone else for your own feeling. Example: "I'm not angry, you're angry."
Displacement: redirecting emotion to a safer target. Example: angry at your boss, so you yell at your dog.
Rationalization: making up a logical-sounding excuse. Example: "I didn't study because the test was probably easy anyway."
Sublimation: channeling an urge into something acceptable. Example: turning anger into a hard workout.

A mnemonic for the order: Really Puzzling Dreams Ruin Sleep (Repression, Projection, Displacement, Rationalization, Sublimation).

Then try this: cover the names, read the example, and say which mechanism it is. Repeat until you get them all right, and say the mnemonic aloud a few times.

turns.q: what's the best way to study for a nursing exam
turns.expect: Recommends practice questions, active recall, applying concepts to patient scenarios, and spaced review.
turns.ans:
The most effective way to study for a nursing exam is to practise pulling information out of your head, not just rereading it.

Active recall: Close your notes and write down everything you remember about a topic, then check what you missed.
Spaced repetition: Review material in short sessions spread over several days. Flashcards work well for drug names, definitions and normal values.
Practice questions: Do NCLEX-style questions, and for each one, explain why the right answer is right and why the others are wrong. The reasoning matters more than the answer.
Work through care scenarios: Ask yourself what you would assess, what the priority is, what you would do first, and what you would tell the patient. Nursing exams test judgment, so practise applying facts to a patient.
Concept maps: Link conditions, causes, signs, interventions and rationales. This helps with the "why" behind each nursing action.
Teach it back: Explain a topic out loud as if to a classmate. Gaps show up quickly.
Sleep and short breaks: Memory consolidates while you sleep, so a steady routine beats a single long cram session.

turns.q: teach me the cardiac cycle like i'm 5
turns.expect: Gives a simple explanation of the heart squeezing (systole) and relaxing to fill (diastole) with the SA node as the pacemaker.
turns.ans:
Think of your heart as a little pump with two rooms on top and two rooms on the bottom. Every heartbeat is one trip around the cycle.

Rest and fill (diastole): The heart relaxes, like a balloon before you squeeze it. Blood flows in from the body and lungs and fills the rooms.
Squeeze and push (systole): The heart squeezes, like pressing the balloon, and pushes blood out to the lungs and the rest of the body.

What makes it happen:

A tiny spot in the top right of the heart, called the SA node, is the heart's natural drummer. It sends out an electric signal.
The signal makes the top rooms squeeze first, pushing blood down into the bottom rooms.
The signal then waits a tiny moment at the AV node, so the top rooms finish before the bottom rooms squeeze.
Then the signal zooms down special wires to the bottom rooms, which squeeze hard and push blood out.
Then everything relaxes and fills again, and the next beat starts.

So: fill, squeeze, relax, repeat. A resting heart does this about 60 to 100 times a minute.

Sublimation is a defense mechanism in which unacceptable urges, often aggressive or sexual ones, are redirected into socially acceptable, constructive activities. Freud considered it one of the healthiest defenses because the energy still gets an outlet.

turns.expect: From notes: making excuses that sound logical.
turns.ans:
Rationalization is a defense mechanism where a person makes excuses that sound logical to explain away a behavior, feeling, or mistake, so the real reason stays hidden, even from themselves.

For example, someone who failed an exam might say, "The test was unfair anyway, so it doesn't matter that I didn't study." The excuse sounds reasonable, but it protects their self-image from the real cause.

In nursing, it helps to notice it in yourself and in patients, since it can hide a problem that needs addressing.

turns.expect: The SA node.
turns.ans: The natural pacemaker of the heart is the sinoatrial (SA) node, a small cluster of specialized cells in the upper wall of the right atrium. It fires electrical impulses spontaneously, around 60 to 100 times a minute at rest. The impulse spreads through the atria, pauses briefly at the atrioventricular (AV) node, then travels down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to make the ventricles contract.

turns.expect: Ventricles contract and eject blood.
turns.ans: In systole, the ventricles contract and eject blood out of the heart: into the lungs from the right ventricle and into the body from the left ventricle. It's the pumping phase of the cardiac cycle, and it follows the atria contracting and pushing blood down into the ventricles. Diastole is the relaxing phase that follows, when the ventricles fill again.

turns.q: what are the phases of the therapeutic relationship
turns.expect: Peplau's phases: orientation, working (identification/exploitation), termination/resolution; notes the note is truncated.
turns.ans:
The therapeutic relationship has three phases, from Hildegard Peplau's model:

Orientation: The nurse and patient meet, build trust, identify the patient's needs or problem, and agree on goals.
Working: The nurse and patient work together on the agreed goals. This is where the patient explores feelings and changes behaviour, and where transference and countertransference can come up.
Termination: The relationship ends once goals are met or the patient no longer needs care. The nurse and patient review progress and prepare for separation.

turns.q: explain displacement with a nursing example
turns.expect: Gives a clinical example of a patient redirecting anger to a safer target.
turns.ans:
Displacement is a defense mechanism where a person redirects strong feelings from the real source to a safer target. The feeling is real, but the person hasn't been able to express it toward the person who caused it.

Nursing example: A patient is furious that his surgeon has delayed his discharge again. He can't safely confront the surgeon, who controls his care, so when the nurse comes in to check his blood pressure, he snaps, "Why is everything here so slow?" The anger belongs to the surgeon, but the nurse is the safer target because she is there and less likely to retaliate.

A nurse who recognizes displacement can stay calm and avoid taking it personally. She might say, "I can see you're frustrated about waiting. Let me check with the team about your discharge timing." Acknowledging the feeling and redirecting the patient toward the real issue helps without shutting him down.

turns.q: go through transference and the id with me
turns.expect: Studies those two Psych Nursing Terms cards with the student.
turns.ans:
Let's start with the id, since it's the foundation of Freud's model of personality.

The id

It's the primitive, unconscious part of the mind.
It runs on the pleasure principle: it seeks immediate gratification of basic drives (hunger, comfort, anger, sexual and aggressive urges) and doesn't care about consequences or reality.
It's present from birth. The ego and superego develop later.
The ego mediates between the id and reality (the reality principle), and the superego pushes back with moral rules and guilt.

Transference

This is when a patient unconsciously redirects feelings they had toward someone important in their past (a parent, sibling or former partner) onto the nurse.
The feelings can be positive (the patient sees the nurse as a caring parent) or negative (the patient reacts with anger or distrust that really belongs to someone else).
The patient isn't doing it on purpose and usually isn't aware of it.

How the two connect

Transference is about feelings that were never fully worked through in the past. Those feelings often come from unmet needs or strong drives, so the id's wishes can show up in how the patient relates to the nurse.

What the nurse does

Recognize that the feelings are about the patient's history, not about the nurse personally.
Stay professional and respond calmly rather than taking it personally.
Set clear boundaries and keep the focus on the patient's needs.
Watch for countertransference (the nurse's own emotional reaction to the patient, based on the nurse's past) and seek supervision if it's affecting care.

turns.q: i didnt get transference in class
turns.expect: Reassures them and briefly explains transference accurately from their notes (patient redirects past feelings onto the nurse).
turns.ans:
Transference is when a patient unconsciously redirects feelings they had toward someone from their past onto the nurse. The patient might have a parent, ex, or old boss in mind, but the feelings land on you.

For example, a patient who grew up feeling ignored by their father might keep asking the nurse for constant reassurance, or get angry at the nurse over small things. The patient isn't really reacting to you, but to that old relationship.

The nurse's job is to notice the pattern, stay calm and professional, and not take it personally. Transference can also be a useful clue about what the patient needs. Nurses who spot it can talk it through with a supervisor. The nurse's own reaction to the patient is called countertransference.

Your Psych Nursing Terms deck has a card on this, so you can check your understanding there. Do you want me to quiz you on it?

turns.expect: Confirms warmly and maybe contrasts with countertransference briefly.

Once you see the pattern, it usually clicks. Your 'i feel dumb' earlier didn't match what you just did, because you asked about something you didn't get and kept going until it made sense. A quick way to remember it: the id wants, the superego judges, and the ego decides what's realistic.

turns.q: it's about what the SA node does
turns.expect: Guides them toward the answer using their notes (natural pacemaker) in a supportive way.
turns.ans:
The SA (sinoatrial) node is the heart's natural pacemaker. It's a small cluster of specialized cells in the upper wall of the right atrium that fires electrical impulses on its own, about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest.

Each impulse spreads across both atria, making them contract and push blood into the ventricles. The signal then reaches the AV node, which briefly delays it so the ventricles can fill. From there it travels through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, making the ventricles contract and eject blood.

turns.expect: Confirms and adds the conduction path from their notes (AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers).
turns.ans: Yes. The SA node starts each heartbeat. It spontaneously generates an electrical impulse, which spreads across the atria and makes them contract. The signal then pauses briefly at the AV node, travels down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers, and triggers the ventricles to contract. Because the SA node sets the pace, it's the heart's natural pacemaker. If it stopped, a slower backup pacemaker elsewhere in the heart could take over.

turns.expect: Explains briefly using the MAIN causes from their notes.

*sets down my teacup with a heavy sigh* The shots in Sarajevo were the spark, but the powder had been stacked for years. Gavrilo Princip was a young Bosnian Serb who belonged to a nationalist group, and he wanted Bosnia taken from Austria-Hungary. Vienna decided to answer with force.

In July 1914 my government sent Serbia an ultimatum with harsh demands. Serbia accepted most of them but not all, and on 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. Russia, Serbia's protector, began to mobilise its army. Germany, our ally, had already promised its support to Vienna, so it declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France two days later, then marched through neutral Belgium. Britain entered the war on 4 August, when Germany's invasion of Belgium broke the treaty guaranteeing Belgian neutrality.

So one assassination set off a chain of alliances, each nation bound to the next. A local quarrel in the Balkans became a war across Europe within five weeks. I would not wish that lesson on anyone, least of all a student with an essay to write.
